title: Old land, young nation
description: People reached the Americas thousands of years before the United States declared independence in 1776.

facts.text: The first Americans arrived about 25,000 to 15,000 years ago.

title: Turning points of US history
description: Independence (1776), the Constitution (1787), the Civil War (1861 to 1865) and the end of slavery (1865), Pearl Harbor (1941) and the Moon landing (1969).

facts.text: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
The US Constitution was written in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 and signed on September 17, 1787.
The American Civil War (1861 to 1865) was fought between the United States and 11 Southern states that seceded and formed the Confederacy.
The 13th Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865, abolished slavery in the United States.
Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, brought the United States into World War II.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts became the first people to walk on the Moon.

title: From 13 colonies to 50 states
description: The Declaration spoke for 13 British colonies; Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959.

facts.text: The Declaration of Independence announced the separation of 13 British colonies in North America from Great Britain.
Hawaii became the 50th US state on August 21, 1959.

title: Across Beringia
description: During the last Ice Age, lower seas exposed Beringia, linking Siberia and Alaska; many scientists think people crossed it from East Asia, while others propose a coastal route by boat.

facts.text: During the last Ice Age, so much water was frozen in glaciers that sea levels fell by as much as about 400 feet, exposing Beringia, dry land where the Bering Strait's seafloor is now, linking Siberia and Alaska.
Many scientists think people crossed from East Asia into North America over the Bering Land Bridge, following the animals they hunted.
Some scientists propose that early peoples reached the Americas by boat or along a coastal route instead.

title: When the first Americans came
description: For decades Clovis (about 13,000 years ago) was thought to be first; Monte Verde, accepted in 1997, proved people came earlier; the White Sands footprints (about 21,000 to 23,000 years) are still debated.

facts.text: The Clovis culture is known for leaf-shaped, fluted stone spear points.
For decades, Clovis artifacts, about 13,000 years old, were the oldest known in the Americas, so many archaeologists thought the Clovis people were the first Americans.
Monte Verde, a campsite in southern Chile, shows people living there more than 14,000 years ago, earlier than Clovis.
Archaeologists broadly accepted Monte Verde's early date in 1997.
Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago.
Some archaeologists remain skeptical of the White Sands dates, arguing the dated material may seem older than it is.

title: Hundreds of languages
description: At European contact North America north of Mexico had about 300 languages; California alone showed more variety than all of Europe.

facts.text: At European contact, North America north of Mexico had about 300 distinct languages.
According to the linguist Edward Sapir, the languages of California alone showed more variety than all of Europe's.

title: Many ways of life
description: Anthropologists group Native North America into culture areas; some peoples hunted and gathered, others farmed; Northwest Coast peoples lived on abundant salmon; farming peoples planted corn, beans and squash together.

facts.text: Anthropologists group Native North America into culture areas, regions where similar ways of life occurred, such as the Northeast, the Plains, the Southwest and the Northwest Coast.
Many Native peoples lived by hunting and gathering, while others were farmers.
Northwest Coast peoples had abundant, reliable supplies of salmon and other fish, sea mammals and shellfish, and built large houses of timber planks.
Many farming peoples planted corn, beans and squash together; the Iroquois and the Cherokee called them the three sisters.
In a three sisters field, corn stalks support the beans, beans add nitrogen to the soil, and squash leaves shade out weeds and keep the soil moist.

title: Cahokia, a city north of Mexico
description: Cahokia, near St. Louis, flourished about 950 to 1350 on corn farming, held perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people around 1100, and declined probably through environmental damage.

facts.text: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the largest urban center north of Mexico and flourished from about 950 to 1350.
Most people at Cahokia were farmers, and corn (maize) was the center of their farming.
At its peak, around 1100, Cahokia had perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 people, probably a little more than London at the time.
Cahokia declined probably because of environmental damage, as cutting forests brought erosion and flooding; disease, climate change, social stress and warfare may also have played a part.

title: Cahokia's mounds
description: Cahokia's earthen mounds were built basket by basket; Monks Mound rises about 100 feet with a base like the Great Pyramid's and once held a large building, likely the seat of government; Woodhenge worked as a calendar.

facts.text: Cahokia's mounds were built of earth carried to the site basket by basket.
Monks Mound rises about 100 feet, its base is about the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza's, and it is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas.
A building about 100 feet long once stood on top of Monks Mound, believed to be the seat of Cahokia's government.
At Woodhenge, circles of wooden posts lined up with the rising sun at certain times of the year, so they served as a calendar.

title: Chaco's great houses
description: Ancestral Puebloans, ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples, built Chaco Canyon's multistory stone great houses from the mid-800s; Pueblo Bonito held over 600 rooms and roads linked Chaco to 150 great houses.

facts.text: The older name Anasazi comes from Navajo; Pueblo people consider it disrespectful and prefer Ancestral Puebloans.
In Chaco Canyon, in today's New Mexico, Chacoan culture flourished from the mid-800s for more than 300 years.
Chacoans built great houses: massive stone buildings of several stories with hundreds of rooms, often oriented to the sun, the moon and the cardinal directions.
Pueblo Bonito, the largest great house, was D-shaped, stood four to five stories tall and held over 600 rooms.
Roads linked Chaco Canyon's great houses to more than 150 great houses across the region.

title: Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings
description: At Mesa Verde the ancestors of Pueblo people built cliff dwellings in canyon alcoves from about 1180 to 1300, then moved south after the Great Drought; their descendants are today's Pueblo peoples.

facts.text: At Mesa Verde, in today's Colorado, the ancestors of Pueblo people built most of their cliff dwellings between about 1180 and 1300, in alcoves in the canyon walls.
Cliff Palace is the largest cliff dwelling in North America.
By 1300, after the Great Drought of 1276 to 1299, most people had left Mesa Verde, moving south into what is now New Mexico and Arizona.
The people of Mesa Verde are among the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples.

title: The Great Law of Peace
description: The Peacemaker and Hiawatha joined the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca under the Great Law: 50 chiefs chosen by Clan Mothers, one vote per nation, unanimous decisions.

facts.text: Haudenosaunee means People of the Longhouse; the confederacy's five original nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca.
Haudenosaunee tradition credits the Peacemaker, helped by Hiawatha (Aionwatha), with founding the confederacy under the Great Law of Peace.
The Hiawatha Belt records how the five warring nations buried their weapons of war under the Tree of Peace, planted in Onondaga territory.
Wampum beads are made of white and purple shell, and the designs and colors of wampum belts are memory aids for history, traditions and laws.
Under the Great Law of Peace, 50 peace chiefs shared authority over civil affairs; each nation had one vote, and decisions had to be unanimous.
Each nation's chiefs are chosen by Clan Mothers.
After the Tuscarora joined in 1722, the confederacy became known to the English as the Six Nations.

Scholars disagree on when the confederacy formed: most place it in the mid to late 1400s, while Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields argue for 1142, the year of a solar eclipse that may match a sign in the sky in the oral tradition.

title: Did the League shape the Constitution?
description: Canassatego (1744) and Franklin (1751) linked the League to colonial union, and Congress acknowledged its contribution in 1988, but historians still argue how much it shaped the Constitution.

facts.text: At a 1744 treaty meeting, the Onondaga leader Canassatego urged the colonies to unite, and in 1751 Benjamin Franklin argued that if the Six Nations could form such a union, a dozen English colonies should manage one too.

In 1988, on the Constitution's 200th anniversary, Congress passed a resolution acknowledging the contribution of the Iroquois Confederacy and other Indian nations to the formation and development of the United States.
Historians argue over whether the confederacy influenced the Constitution; skeptics say European political theory supplied the Founders' models and the evidence for Native influence is thin.
The historians Donald Grinde and Bruce Johansen argue that Iroquois and other Native political ideas helped shape American government, including the Constitution.

title: What crossed the Atlantic
description: After 1492 American crops like corn, potatoes and tomatoes spread worldwide, while horses, cattle, pigs and wheat came to the Americas; horses transformed Plains bison hunting.

facts.text: The Columbian Exchange is the transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world that followed Columbus's voyage of 1492.
The name comes from the historian Alfred W. Crosby's 1972 book The Columbian Exchange, which sorted the exchange into diseases, animals and plants.
Farmers of the Americas gave the world corn (maize), potatoes, cassava and sweet potatoes, plus tomatoes, peanuts, squashes, pineapples and chili peppers.
Horses, pigs, cattle, goats and sheep adapted readily to the Americas, and wheat, rice, rye and barley prospered there too.
On horseback, Plains peoples could hunt bison far more successfully, boosting their food supplies until the 1870s, when the bison dwindled.

title: Epidemics in the Americas
description: The Americas had none of Eurasia's crowd diseases such as smallpox and measles, so Native peoples had no past exposure; populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650.

facts.text: Before 1492, the Americas had none of the acute infectious diseases, such as smallpox, measles and influenza, that had long troubled Eurasia and Africa; many came from herd animals like cattle and pigs, which the first Americans had not domesticated.
Across the Americas, populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650, largely because of epidemics.

title: Spain comes north
description: Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously occupied European-founded US city, and colonized New Mexico from 1598, with Santa Fe as capital from 1610.

facts.text: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine, Florida, on September 8, 1565; it is the oldest continuously occupied city founded by Europeans in the United States.
Spain acted in Florida partly because France was trying to build permanent settlements there.
In 1598 Juan de Oñate led an expedition of settlers, priests and soldiers into today's New Mexico.
Santa Fe became the capital of Spanish New Mexico in 1610.

title: The Pueblo Revolt
description: After decades of religious persecution, forced labor and hunger, Po'pay coordinated the pueblos with knotted cords; on August 10, 1680 they rose and drove the Spanish out until 1692.

facts.text: Spanish missionaries forced Catholicism on the Pueblo peoples and burned their kivas, masks and other sacred objects, and Pueblo people suffered forced labor and hunger.
Po'pay, a religious leader from San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh), had been imprisoned and flogged by the Spanish before he planned the revolt.
Runners carried knotted cords to the pueblos; one knot was untied each day, and the revolt would begin when the last was untied.
On August 10, 1680, almost all the Pueblos rose together; by August 21 the Spanish had fled, leaving about 400 dead, including 21 priests.
The revolt forced the Spanish to retreat south to what is now El Paso, Texas.
The Pueblos stayed free until 1692, when Diego de Vargas retook New Mexico for Spain.

title: Jamestown barely survives
description: Jamestown (1607), the first permanent English settlement, sat on an unhealthy marshy site and nearly died in the Starving Time of 1609 to 1610.

facts.text: Jamestown, founded on May 14, 1607, by the Virginia Company of London, was the first permanent English settlement in North America.
Jamestown's marshy site proved unhealthy: bad river water, mosquitoes and short rations brought dysentery and fevers.
In the Starving Time, the winter of 1609 to 1610, drought, a Powhatan siege and scarce supplies left only about 60 of some 500 colonists alive.
In June 1610 the survivors boarded ships to go home, but an incoming fleet ordered them to turn back.

title: Tobacco makes Jamestown pay
description: John Rolfe's West Indies tobacco, first shipped in 1614, made the colony profitable and drove settlers onto Native land.

facts.text: John Rolfe replaced Virginia's harsh native tobacco with milder plants from the West Indies; after he shipped his first barrels to England in 1614, other colonists saw his lucrative results and copied him.
Profitable tobacco led settlers to press further into Native territory for rich new land.

title: The Powhatan chiefdom
description: Powhatan (Wahunsenacawh) ruled Tsenacomoco, dozens of tribes; peace came with Pocahontas's 1614 marriage to Rolfe, and war in 1622 when Opechancanough struck the spreading colony.

facts.text: Powhatan, whose given name was Wahunsenacawh, was paramount chief of Tsenacomoco in tidewater Virginia; he united dozens of tribes, more than 150 towns paid him tribute, and he was the highest authority in the region when the English built Jamestown.
John Rolfe married Powhatan's daughter Pocahontas in April 1614, and the marriage brought peace between the Powhatans and the English.
John Smith claimed that Pocahontas saved his life; some writers think he misunderstood a ceremony, and others say he invented the rescue.
In 1622 Powhatan warriors led by Opechancanough, Powhatan's brother and successor, struck the colony, killing 347 of about 1,200 English colonists.

title: Europeans enter a crowded continent
description: Spain and England built their first towns in lands already ruled by Native nations; St. Augustine was 42 years older than Jamestown, and epidemics reshaped the continent.

facts.text: St. Augustine, founded in 1565, is 42 years older than Jamestown, founded in 1607.

title: The Wampanoag-Plymouth alliance
description: An epidemic of 1616 to 1619 emptied Patuxet, where Plymouth was built in 1620; Ousamequin (Massasoit) allied with Plymouth in 1621 against the Narragansett, and Tisquantum interpreted.

facts.text: Between 1616 and 1619 an epidemic ravaged the Wampanoag and neighboring peoples, emptying Tisquantum's home village of Patuxet.
The Mayflower colonists founded Plymouth in 1620 on the site of Patuxet.
The epidemic left the Wampanoag vulnerable to the Narragansett, who had escaped it; English guns and soldiers could help against them.
In 1621 the Wampanoag leader Ousamequin, called Massasoit by the English, and Plymouth agreed to defend each other and to trade.
Tisquantum (Squanto) of Patuxet was kidnapped by an English captain to be sold as a slave in Spain, escaped to England and learned English.
Tisquantum came home in 1619 to find his people wiped out by disease, and later served Plymouth as its interpreter.

title: The 1621 harvest and the Thanksgiving story
description: In fall 1621 about 90 Wampanoag men and about 50 colonists shared a harvest celebration over several days; the national Thanksgiving holiday dates from 1863, and since 1970 some Native people mark a National Day of Mourning.

facts.text: In fall 1621 about 90 Wampanoag men led by Ousamequin joined about 50 colonists at Plymouth's harvest celebration for several days, bringing venison.
The 1621 gathering is commonly called the first Thanksgiving, but Lincoln proclaimed Thanksgiving a national holiday only in 1863.
Since 1970 Native people and supporters have gathered at Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day for a National Day of Mourning.

title: A city upon a hill
description: In 1630 John Winthrop led Puritans to found the Massachusetts Bay Colony, a model community with a purified church that he said would be watched as a city upon a hill.

facts.text: In 1630 John Winthrop, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, led a fleet of mostly Puritan settlers to New England.
The Puritans wanted a godly society and a church purified of what they saw as corruptions in the Church of England.
In his 1630 sermon A Model of Christian Charity, Winthrop said the colony would be "a city upon a hill", with all the world watching it.

title: Banished dissenters
description: Massachusetts banished Roger Williams in 1635 for his views on conscience and Native land; he founded Providence. Anne Hutchinson, convicted in 1637, went to Aquidneck in 1638.

facts.text: Roger Williams argued that magistrates had no right to rule consciences, and that Native people, not the king's charter, truly owned the land.
Massachusetts banished Williams in 1635; the Narragansett sold him land, and he founded Providence, open to people of all faiths.
Anne Hutchinson held weekly meetings of Boston women to discuss sermons and share her own religious views.
Convicted in 1637 of slandering the colony's ministers, Hutchinson was banished and in 1638 helped found a settlement on Aquidneck, now in Rhode Island.

title: Three colonial regions
description: New England lived by small farms, fishing, shipbuilding and trade; the Middle Colonies were the grain-growing breadbasket; the Southern Colonies grew tobacco, rice and indigo with enslaved labor.

facts.text: New England's rocky soil and cold winters suited small family farms, so colonists turned to fishing, lumbering, shipbuilding and trade.
The Middle Colonies were called the breadbasket colonies: their fertile soil grew enough wheat and other grain to export.
The Middle Colonies drew an unusually diverse mix of settlers, including Germans and Scots-Irish as well as English.
In the Chesapeake colonies of Virginia and Maryland planters grew tobacco; in the Carolinas and Georgia, rice and indigo.
Southern plantations came to rely on the forced labor of enslaved Africans.

title: Pennsylvania's holy experiment
description: In 1681 Charles II granted the Quaker William Penn a charter for Pennsylvania, which Penn opened to people of all faiths.

facts.text: In 1681 Charles II granted the Quaker William Penn a charter for Pennsylvania, which Penn opened to people of all faiths.

title: The first Africans in English Virginia
description: In 1619 the White Lion brought 20 and odd Africans to Point Comfort, Virginia; their legal status was unclear, and some, like Anthony Johnson, became free landowners.

facts.text: In late August 1619 the English ship White Lion brought "20 and odd" Africans to Point Comfort, Virginia.
The legal status of these first Africans in Virginia is unclear: they may have been enslaved for life or freed after years of service.
Anthony Johnson, listed as "Antonio the Negro" in 1625, gained his freedom and became a landowner among free Africans in Northampton County.

title: Slavery written into law
description: Colonial courts and laws made slavery race-based and lifelong (John Punch), legal (Massachusetts, 1641) and inherited through the mother (Virginia, 1662).

facts.text: After three servants ran away in Virginia, a court gave the two white men extra years, but sentenced John Punch, an African, to serve for life.
In 1641 Massachusetts became the first English colony to legalize slavery, in its Body of Liberties.
A 1662 Virginia law made a child enslaved or free according to the mother's status, reversing the English rule that status followed the father.

title: The scale of the Middle Passage
description: SlaveVoyages estimates about 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard ships and about 10.7 million survived; about 388,000 landed directly in mainland North America.

facts.text: SlaveVoyages database estimates: about 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard ships to the Americas, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing.
The gap between those two estimates means roughly 1.8 million people died during the Middle Passage.
About 388,000 survivors were landed directly in mainland North America, a small share; most were landed in the Caribbean and South America.

title: Enduring and resisting the Middle Passage
description: Olaudah Equiano's 1789 narrative describes captives chained below deck amid filth and death; captives revolted on about one ship in ten.

facts.text: Olaudah Equiano, once enslaved and later free, wrote in his 1789 autobiography of captives kept below deck in chains and filth, amid "the shrieks of the women, and the groans of the dying".
Captives rose in revolt on about one slave ship in ten, most often while the ship was still near the African coast; few revolts succeeded.

title: Why Metacom went to war
description: Metacom, Massasoit's son, recorded grievances over lost land, English cattle and unequal courts; Plymouth's execution of three Wampanoag men in 1675 set off the war.

facts.text: Metacom, whom the English called King Philip, was a Wampanoag sachem and a son of Massasoit, who had greeted Plymouth's colonists in 1621.
In June 1675 Metacom told John Easton of Rhode Island his people's complaints: lost land, English cattle ruining their crops, unfair English courts.
The war began after Plymouth hanged three Wampanoag men in June 1675 for the murder of John Sassamon, a Christian convert and interpreter.
The Wampanoag, Nipmuc and Narragansett fought the colonists, while the Mohegan and Pequot fought alongside the English.

title: What King Philip's War cost
description: Metacom was killed in August 1676; about 600 English soldiers died and 17 settlements were destroyed, while thousands of Native people died and many were sold into slavery.

facts.text: Colonial forces under Benjamin Church killed Metacom in August 1676.
About 600 English colonists were killed and many towns destroyed; thousands of Native people were killed, and many were sold into slavery.
For the size of the population, King Philip's War was one of the bloodiest wars in American history.

title: Coverture and women's work
description: Under coverture a married woman's legal identity merged into her husband's; unmarried women and widows (femes soles) could own property and run businesses; households ran on women's work.

facts.text: Under coverture, from English law, a married woman's legal existence merged into her husband's: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name.
Unmarried women and widows, called femes soles, could own property, make contracts and run businesses in their own names.
Colonial households ran on women's work: cooking, cleaning, spinning, weaving, sewing, and making butter and soap.

title: Eliza Lucas Pinckney and indigo
description: At 16 Eliza Lucas managed her father's South Carolina plantations and developed indigo, which became the colony's second most lucrative crop, grown and processed by enslaved people.

facts.text: Around 1739 Eliza Lucas, 16, was left to manage her father's Wappoo Plantation near Charleston and two larger South Carolina estates.
After trying crops such as ginger and cotton, she grew a successful indigo crop, and indigo became South Carolina's second most lucrative crop after rice.
In colonial South Carolina, enslaved people did almost all the work of growing indigo and turning it into dye, skilled work learned through long experience.

title: Colonial assemblies and town meetings
description: Virginia's House of Burgesses (1619), the Mayflower Compact (1620) and New England town meetings gave colonists elected self-government, though voting was limited to property-owning white men.

facts.text: Virginia's House of Burgesses first met at Jamestown on July 30, 1619, the first elected assembly in English America.
Before landing in 1620, 41 men aboard the Mayflower signed the Mayflower Compact, forming a "civil body politic" to make laws.
In New England town meetings, a town's voters gathered to elect local officials and vote on taxes and spending.
Colonial voters were usually white men who owned property; women, enslaved people and Native people were shut out.

title: Salutary neglect and the power of the purse
description: Britain loosely enforced its rules (Burke's 'salutary neglect'), and colonial assemblies controlled taxes and governors' salaries.

facts.text: Colonial assemblies controlled taxes and spending, including the royal governor's salary, which they could withhold.
In 1775 Edmund Burke credited the colonies' success to Britain's "wise and salutary neglect": its loose enforcement of rules.

title: The French and Indian War
description: From 1754 to 1763 Britain and France, each with Native allies, fought for eastern North America as part of the Seven Years' War; Franklin's Albany Plan failed; Britain won Canada and the land east of the Mississippi.

facts.text: In 1754 George Washington led Virginia troops to drive the French from the Ohio Valley; outnumbered, he surrendered at Fort Necessity.
The French and Indian War (1754 to 1763) was the North American part of a wider war between Britain and France, the Seven Years' War.
France fought with many Native allies, such as the Shawnee, while Britain's main Native partner was the Iroquois Confederacy.
At Albany in 1754, Benjamin Franklin proposed uniting the colonies under one council; the colonial assemblies and the Crown rejected it.
In the 1763 Treaty of Paris, Britain gained Canada and all French lands east of the Mississippi, and Florida from Spain.

title: Victory and debt
description: The war nearly doubled Britain's debt, and Britain wanted the colonies to help pay; Pontiac's War of 1763 led Britain to bar settlement west of the Appalachians.

facts.text: The war nearly doubled Britain's national debt, and Britain expected the colonies to help pay it off.
In 1763 Native nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley attacked British forts in Pontiac's War; Britain then barred colonists from settling farther west.

title: Freedom and slavery from the same year
description: In 1619 Virginia gained both the first elected assembly in English America and its first recorded Africans: self-government and slavery grew up together in the colonies.

facts.text: Virginia's first elected assembly and its first recorded Africans both arrived in 1619, a year before Plymouth was founded.

title: The Stamp Act crisis
description: The 1765 tax on printed paper, the colonial argument of no taxation without consent, the boycott and the repeal of 1766.

facts.text: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed colonial legal papers, newspapers, pamphlets, playing cards and dice, which had to carry a stamp showing the tax was paid.
Britain passed the Stamp Act to help pay the heavy cost of defending its American colonies after the French and Indian War.
Colonists argued that they could be taxed only with their own consent, through their own representatives, and they had none in Parliament.
The Sons of Liberty formed in the summer of 1765 to oppose the Stamp Act and destroyed the stamps wherever they found them.
Delegates from nine colonies met in New York in October 1765 as the Stamp Act Congress and petitioned against the tax.
Colonists boycotted British goods, and British merchants whose sales fell pressed Parliament, which repealed the Stamp Act on March 18, 1766.

title: Parliament's answer: virtual representation
description: Britain argued Parliament represented all Britons, voters or not, and asserted in the Declaratory Act its power over the colonies in all cases.

facts.text: Britain answered that every member of Parliament represented the whole nation, even English cities like Manchester that elected no members: virtual representation.
Colonists rejected virtual representation: in their view, a Parliament they did not elect could not consent to taxes for them.
On the day it repealed the Stamp Act, Parliament passed the Declaratory Act, claiming power to bind the colonies "in all cases whatsoever".

title: From the Townshend duties to the Tea Party
description: Townshend duties, troops in Boston, the Boston Massacre and the Tea Party of 1773.

facts.text: In 1767 the Townshend Acts put duties on lead, glass, paper, paint and tea imported into the colonies.
Two British regiments arrived in Boston in October 1768 to keep order in the resisting town.
On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston, killing five colonists, among them Crispus Attucks, a Black sailor who had likely been enslaved.
John Adams defended the soldiers in court, arguing they had a right to defend themselves; six of the eight were acquitted.
The Tea Act of 1773 let the East India Company sell tea more cheaply in the colonies, but the tax on tea stayed in place.
On December 16, 1773, men disguised as Native Americans boarded ships in Boston Harbor and dumped about 340 chests of tea overboard.

title: The Intolerable Acts unite the colonies
description: Parliament's 1774 punishment of Boston backfired, bringing the colonies together in the First Continental Congress.

facts.text: In 1774 Parliament closed the port of Boston until the destroyed tea was paid for, and replaced Massachusetts' elected council with an appointed one.
The Intolerable Acts rallied the colonies: on September 5, 1774, delegates from every colony but Georgia met in Philadelphia and called for a boycott of British goods.

title: Minutemen and the alarm
description: Massachusetts patriots organized militia, minutemen and an alarm system before April 1775.

facts.text: In 1774 Massachusetts patriots formed a Provincial Congress, which took control of the colony's militia and stockpiled arms, ammunition and provisions.
In October 1774 the Provincial Congress urged towns to raise minutemen, volunteers who trained and would be ready at a minute's notice.
Prearranged lantern signals showed whether the British went by water or land, and Paul Revere, William Dawes and Samuel Prescott rode to spread the alarm.

title: Lexington and Concord
description: The first battles of April 19, 1775, and the British retreat that began the Siege of Boston.

facts.text: General Thomas Gage ordered British troops to march from Boston and seize the colonists' military stores at Concord.
At Lexington on April 19, 1775, the British volley killed 8 colonial militiamen and wounded 10.
At Concord's North Bridge, militia fired on a British party and forced it to withdraw.
Militia fired on the British from behind houses, barns, trees and stone walls all the way back to Boston, and thousands of New Englanders then besieged the city.

title: Common Sense's argument
description: Thomas Paine's 1776 pamphlet argued in plain language against kings and for independence.

facts.text: Thomas Paine came to the colonies from England in November 1774 with letters of introduction from Benjamin Franklin.
Paine published Common Sense on January 10, 1776, arguing for American independence and against monarchy.
Paine wrote in plain language and attacked hereditary rule: no one, he argued, had a right by birth to set his family above all others.
Paine wrote: "there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island."

title: How Common Sense spread
description: The pamphlet was read aloud to listeners, and historians debate how many copies really sold.

facts.text: Common Sense was short enough to be read aloud, and people read it in taverns and on street corners to listeners who could not read.
Common Sense is often called America's first best-seller.
Paine claimed about 120,000 copies sold in three months; historian Trish Loughran, counting 25 printings of at most 3,000 each, puts the limit near 75,000.

title: The Declaration's argument
description: Rights, equality, government by consent and a list of grievances, voted in July 1776.

facts.text: In June 1776 Congress chose Jefferson, John Adams, Franklin, Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston to draft a declaration; Jefferson wrote the draft.
On July 2, 1776, Congress voted that the colonies "are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states."
The Declaration says: "We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal."
The Declaration says governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed," and people may "alter or to abolish" a destructive one.
Most of the Declaration is a list of grievances charging King George III with "repeated injuries and usurpations."

title: The Declaration's contradiction
description: The Declaration's equality clashed with slavery, as Jefferson's cut passage and critics like Samuel Johnson and Prince Hall showed.

facts.text: Jefferson's draft blamed the king for the slave trade, "cruel war against human nature itself," but Congress cut it, to please South Carolina and Georgia, he said.
Thomas Jefferson enslaved more than 600 people over his lifetime.
In 1775 the British writer Samuel Johnson asked: "How is it that we hear the loudest yelps for liberty among the drivers of negroes?"
In January 1777, Prince Hall and seven other Black men petitioned the Massachusetts legislature for freedom as the natural right of all people.

title: Saratoga and the French alliance
description: Burgoyne's surrender in 1777 convinced France to ally with the United States in 1778.

facts.text: On October 17, 1777, near Saratoga, New York, British General John Burgoyne surrendered his whole army to American General Horatio Gates.
Before any alliance, the French government secretly sent the Americans aid through agents.
News of Saratoga persuaded France's foreign minister, the comte de Vergennes, to choose an alliance with the United States.
On February 6, 1778, Benjamin Franklin and two other envoys signed a Treaty of Alliance with France; Spain entered the war against Britain in 1779.

title: Yorktown and the peace
description: French and American forces trapped Cornwallis in 1781; the Treaty of Paris ended the war in 1783.

facts.text: In 1781 Washington and the French general Rochambeau trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown, while a French fleet under de Grasse blocked rescue by sea.
Cornwallis surrendered his army at Yorktown on October 19, 1781, which ended the major fighting of the Revolution.
The State Department's Office of the Historian calls French help crucial to winning the British surrender at Yorktown.
The Treaty of Paris of 1783 formally ended the war between Britain and the United States, France and Spain.

title: The Loyalists
description: Who stayed loyal to the Crown, how many there were, and the tens of thousands who went into exile.

facts.text: Loyalists included royal officeholders, Anglican clergy and their congregations, large landholders, wealthy merchants, and pacifist Quakers.
The trait most Loyalists shared was a cautious conservatism and a deep devotion to Britain and the Crown.
Estimates of how many colonists were Loyalists range from about 15 percent to about a third.
Estimates of how many Loyalists left range from about 60,000 to 100,000; most went to Canada, to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Quebec.

title: Native nations in the Revolution
description: Most Native nations that fought sided with Britain to protect their lands; the Haudenosaunee split; the peace ignored them.

facts.text: Most Native nations that fought sided with Britain, from old alliances and a belief that they had a better chance of keeping their lands under the British.
The Mohawk leader Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea) led Haudenosaunee fighters allied with the British in raids on New York and Pennsylvania settlements.
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy first tried to stay neutral, then split: the Oneida and Tuscarora backed the Americans, most other nations Britain.
Oneida allies carried corn to Washington's starving army at Valley Forge, and Polly Cooper, an Oneida woman, stayed to show soldiers how to cook it.
In the Treaty of Paris of 1783, neither Britain nor the United States made any provision for their Six Nations allies.

title: Enslaved people seek freedom in the war
description: British offers of freedom and American enlistment gave enslaved people paths to freedom on both sides.

facts.text: In November 1775 Lord Dunmore, Virginia's royal governor, promised freedom to servants and enslaved people of rebels who would bear arms for the British.
Thousands of enslaved people escaped to British lines during the war, encouraged by British offers of freedom in 1775 and 1779.
Washington at first barred most Black men from enlisting in the Continental Army, then relented after Dunmore's offer.
In 1778 Rhode Island promised freedom to enslaved men who enlisted in its 1st Rhode Island Regiment.

title: The North begins to end slavery
description: Lawsuits like Elizabeth Freeman's and laws like Pennsylvania's 1780 act began ending slavery in northern states.

facts.text: In 1781 an enslaved woman called Mum Bett sued for freedom under Massachusetts' new constitution; a jury freed her, and she took the name Elizabeth Freeman.
Massachusetts' 1780 constitution declared all men born free and equal, and by 1783 its courts had ruled slavery could not stand there.
Pennsylvania's law of March 1, 1780, the first of its kind, freed no one at once: children later born to enslaved mothers became free at age 28.
Pennsylvania's lawmakers wrote that their own escape from British tyranny obliged them to extend a portion of that freedom to others.
Pennsylvania's act was the first of several northern laws to abolish slavery passed between 1780 and 1804.

title: Women and the boycotts
description: The Daughters of Liberty gave up British goods and spun homespun cloth.

facts.text: During the Stamp Act crisis, women formed the Daughters of Liberty; they gave up tea and held spinning bees to make homespun cloth instead of buying British imports.

title: Women in the war
description: Camp followers kept the armies running, and a few women, like Deborah Sampson, fought.

facts.text: Thousands of women, often soldiers' wives, daughters or mothers, traveled with the armies as camp followers, cooking, washing, sewing and nursing.
In 1782 Deborah Sampson disguised herself as a man and enlisted in the 4th Massachusetts Regiment; a doctor discovered her secret when she fell ill.

title: Remember the ladies
description: Abigail Adams applied the Revolution's argument about representation to women; New Jersey briefly let some women vote.

facts.text: In March 1776 Abigail Adams asked John Adams to "Remember the Ladies" in the new laws, warning against laws "in which we have no voice, or Representation."
New Jersey's 1776 constitution let property-holding inhabitants vote, including unmarried women and widows, until an 1807 law limited voting to free white men.

title: Who gained and who lost by independence
description: Independence rested on consent of the governed, but Loyalists went into exile, Native nations were left out of the peace, and slavery ended only in parts of the North.

facts.text: The Revolutionary War ran from the fighting at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 to the Treaty of Paris of 1783.

title: Why the Articles were weak
description: The Articles of Confederation (in force 1781) gave each state one vote, let Congress only request money and troops, and needed every state to agree to any change.

facts.text: The Articles of Confederation were adopted by Congress in November 1777 but not fully ratified by the states until March 1, 1781.
Under the Articles, Congress could request money and troops from the states but had no power to make them pay.
Under the Articles of Confederation, each state had one vote in Congress.
Any change to the Articles had to be agreed in Congress and then confirmed by the legislatures of every state.

title: Shays’ Rebellion
description: In 1786 and 1787, indebted Massachusetts farmers closed courts and attacked the Springfield arsenal; the crisis convinced many leaders a stronger government was needed.

facts.text: In 1786, armed bands in Massachusetts protesting high taxes and hard times forced courts to close to stop foreclosures and debt cases.
Most of the rebels were farmers in western Massachusetts, many of them Revolutionary War veterans, hit hard by new state taxes.
In January 1787, Daniel Shays led an attack on the federal arsenal at Springfield; it was driven back, and militia routed the rebels at Petersham in February.
The weak national response to Shays’ Rebellion convinced many leaders that a stronger central government was needed, feeding the movement for the Constitutional Convention.

title: The Constitutional Convention and its rival plans
description: Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787; the Virginia Plan wanted representation by population, the New Jersey Plan equal votes for every state.

facts.text: The Constitutional Convention met at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787; 55 delegates took part, and Rhode Island sent none.
George Washington was elected to preside over the Constitutional Convention.
The Virginia Plan, offered by Edmund Randolph, proposed a two-house legislature with each state represented according to its population or wealth.
William Paterson’s New Jersey Plan proposed equal representation for every state in Congress.

title: The Great Compromise
description: Connecticut’s Sherman and Ellsworth proposed a House by population and a Senate with equal seats per state, adopted July 16, 1787, by one vote.

facts.text: The Great Compromise, named for Connecticut delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth, gave the House seats by population and the Senate equal seats for every state.
The Constitutional Convention adopted the Great Compromise on July 16, 1787, by a margin of one vote.
The Constitution gives each state two senators.

title: Slavery in the Constitution’s clauses
description: Without naming slavery, the Constitution counted three-fifths of enslaved people for House seats and taxes, protected the slave trade until 1808 and required escapees to be returned.

facts.text: The Constitution counted three-fifths of the enslaved population when dividing House seats and direct taxes among the states.
Neither the word slave nor the word slavery appears in the original, unamended Constitution.
The Constitution barred Congress from banning the importation of enslaved people before 1808.
The Constitution required that a person “held to Service or Labour” who escaped to another state be “delivered up on Claim.”

title: Arguing over what the Constitution meant for slavery
description: Garrison called the Constitution a proslavery “covenant with death”; after 1851 Douglass argued it could be used to end slavery.

facts.text: On July 4, 1854, at an abolitionist rally in Framingham, Massachusetts, William Lloyd Garrison burned a copy of the Constitution.
Garrison called the Constitution “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell.”
Frederick Douglass once shared Garrison’s view, but in 1851 he broke with him, arguing that the Constitution was a valid legal document that could be used for emancipation.
Douglass argued that the Constitution’s own words, which never named slavery, should be read in favor of liberty, not the framers’ hopes.

title: Federalists and Anti-Federalists
description: Federalists (The Federalist essays) backed the Constitution; Anti-Federalists feared a distant national government and the lack of a bill of rights.

facts.text: The Federalist, 85 essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, appeared in New York newspapers from October 1787 to May 1788 to urge New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution.
Anti-Federalists, including Patrick Henry, feared a single national government, upper-class dominance, weak separation of powers and the loss of local control.
George Mason, a delegate to the Constitutional Convention, refused to sign the Constitution because it lacked a bill of rights.

title: How the ratification fight produced the Bill of Rights
description: Federalists promised amendments to win Massachusetts; Madison introduced them in 1789 and 10 were ratified by 1791.

facts.text: Federalists first argued that a bill of rights was unnecessary because the new government could use only the powers the Constitution listed.
With ratification in danger in Massachusetts, Federalists agreed that the First Congress would consider amendments proposed by the states, which secured ratification there.
James Madison, who had once opposed a bill of rights, introduced a list of amendments in the First Congress on June 8, 1789.
Congress proposed 12 amendments, and by December 15, 1791, the states had ratified 10 of them, now known as the Bill of Rights.
The Anti-Federalists lost the ratification fight, but their agitation led to the addition of the Bill of Rights.

title: Washington’s precedents
description: The only unanimously elected president, Washington created the cabinet, accepted a plain title, warned against parties and retired after two terms.

facts.text: George Washington is the only president elected unanimously by the Electoral College, in both 1789 and 1792.
Among the precedents Washington set was creating the president’s cabinet.
The Senate proposed calling the president “His Highness the President of the United States of America and Protector of their Liberties,” but the House rejected any title and the Senate gave way.
Washington retired after two terms, a precedent every president followed until Franklin D. Roosevelt.
In his Farewell Address of 1796, Washington warned against “the baneful effects of the spirit of party.”

title: Ona Judge’s escape
description: In 1796 Ona Judge escaped slavery in the President’s House in Philadelphia and lived free in New Hampshire despite Washington’s efforts to recapture her.

facts.text: On May 21, 1796, Ona Judge, an enslaved maid, escaped from the President’s House in Philadelphia while George and Martha Washington ate dinner.
Ona Judge had learned that Martha Washington planned to give her to a granddaughter.
Washington tried to have Ona Judge recaptured, but she lived the rest of her life in New Hampshire, legally still a fugitive, until her death in 1848.

title: The fight over the national bank
description: Hamilton’s bank (1791) set Jefferson’s strict reading of Congress’s listed powers against Hamilton’s implied powers.

facts.text: Alexander Hamilton, the first secretary of the Treasury, urged Congress to create a national bank.

After Congress passed a bank bill in February 1791, Washington asked his cabinet, including Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton, whether it was constitutional.
Jefferson argued that the Constitution did not give Congress power to create corporations, including a national bank.
Jefferson warned that going beyond the powers the Constitution gave Congress would be “to take possession of a boundless field of power.”
Hamilton answered that implied powers were delegated as fully as listed ones, so Congress could charter a bank as a means of carrying out its listed powers.
Jefferson pictured a mainly agrarian country and feared the bank would favor financiers and merchants over plantation owners and family farmers.
Washington signed the bank bill in February 1791, and the Bank of the United States opened with a 20-year charter.

title: The first parties
description: Jefferson’s Republicans (Democratic-Republicans) and Hamilton’s Federalists formed in the 1790s over rival visions of the country.

facts.text: Jefferson’s supporters, favoring states’ rights and a strict reading of the Constitution, organized in 1792 as the Republican Party, later called the Democratic-Republicans.
Hamilton’s Federalists favored a strong central government and a loose reading of the Constitution.
The Republicans charged that the Federalists had aristocratic attitudes and that their policies favored the wealthy over ordinary people.

title: The tie of 1800
description: Jefferson and his running mate Burr tied at 73 electoral votes; the House chose Jefferson on the 36th ballot, and the 12th Amendment fixed the rule.

facts.text: Because electors cast two votes without marking which was for president, Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr each received 73 electoral votes.
The House of Representatives broke the tie on February 17, 1801, electing Jefferson on the 36th ballot.
Alexander Hamilton, though a Federalist, worked against Burr and helped build support for Jefferson in the House.
The 12th Amendment, ratified in 1804, gave president and vice president separate electoral votes.

title: The first peaceful transfer between parties
description: In 1801 power passed peacefully from Adams’s Federalists to Jefferson’s Republicans for the first time.

facts.text: In the election of 1800, the Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson defeated the Federalist president, John Adams.
The election of 1800 was the first in which power passed peacefully from one party to another.
In his inaugural address of March 4, 1801, Jefferson said: “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.”

title: The Louisiana Purchase
description: In 1803 the US bought France’s claim to about 828,000 square miles, doubling the country, on land still largely home to Native nations.

facts.text: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana territory, about 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains, from France for $15 million.
The Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the United States.
Jefferson, who favored a strict reading of the Constitution, doubted that it allowed him to buy territory.
The purchase gave the United States France’s imperial claim to land still largely occupied by Native peoples: the sole right to obtain it from them by treaty or conquest.

title: Lewis, Clark and Sacagawea
description: The Corps of Discovery relied on Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman, and her brother Cameahwait’s band for horses to cross the mountains.

facts.text: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led the Corps of Discovery, an expedition that traveled from 1804 to 1806.
Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone woman captured about 1800 by a Hidatsa raiding party and taken to their villages on the Knife River.
Sacagawea, her husband Toussaint Charbonneau and her son Jean Baptiste, born in February 1805, left the Mandan and Hidatsa villages with the Corps that spring.
In August 1805 the expedition met a Shoshone band led by Sacagawea’s brother, Cameahwait, and the reunion helped Lewis and Clark obtain horses to cross the mountains.
Sacagawea was not mainly a guide: she translated with the Shoshone, and her presence signaled the expedition’s peaceful intentions to the nations it met.

title: Why the US fought Britain in 1812
description: Impressment, trade restrictions and British support for Native resistance led to war in 1812; the Treaty of Ghent restored prewar borders.

facts.text: President James Madison signed the declaration of war against Britain on June 18, 1812.
Americans went to war over the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors, British trade restrictions and British support for Native resistance on the frontier.
The Treaty of Ghent, signed on Christmas Eve 1814, restored the prewar boundaries.
The War of 1812 ended without a clear winner, but Indigenous peoples were its real victims, their lands and futures drastically altered.

title: Tecumseh’s confederacy
description: The Shawnee leader Tecumseh built an alliance of Native nations, fought beside Britain and died at the Thames in 1813, ending his hope of a united homeland.

facts.text: The Shawnee leader Tecumseh urged Native nations from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico to set aside rivalries and unite to protect their cultures and lands.
Tecumseh’s younger brother Tenskwatawa, the Prophet, gave the movement spiritual backing, and in 1808 the brothers founded Prophetstown on the Wabash and Tippecanoe rivers.
In November 1811, William Henry Harrison’s force fought the Battle of Tippecanoe and destroyed Prophetstown.
In the War of 1812, Tecumseh allied with the British, and General Isaac Brock placed him in command of all Native forces.
Tecumseh was killed at the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813, and his dream of a unified Native homeland never came to be.

title: A new republic, 1781 to 1815
description: Americans replaced a weak league with a lasting Constitution and peaceful handovers of power, while protecting slavery and pushing into Native lands.

facts.text: Of the 55 delegates who took part in the Constitutional Convention, 39 signed the Constitution.

title: The Cherokee Nation before removal
description: By the 1820s the Cherokee had Sequoyah’s syllabary (1821), a written constitution (1827) and the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper (1828).

facts.text: By 1821 Sequoyah had created a Cherokee writing system of 86 symbols, one for each syllable, and literacy spread quickly.
The Cherokee Nation adopted a written constitution in 1827 and began printing the Cherokee Phoenix, a Native nation's first newspaper, in 1828.

title: Worcester v. Georgia
description: The Indian Removal Act (1830) pressed Southeastern nations west; in 1832 the Supreme Court ruled Georgia law had no force in the Cherokee Nation, but Georgia ignored it and Jackson declined to enforce it.

facts.text: In 1830 Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, pressing Native nations of the Southeast to give up their lands for territory west of the Mississippi.
In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community where Georgia's laws had no force.
Georgia ignored the Worcester ruling, and President Andrew Jackson declined to enforce it.

title: The Trail of Tears
description: A small faction signed the Treaty of New Echota (1835); in 1838 the army forced more than 16,000 Cherokee west, and over 4,000 died by one estimate. Other Southeastern nations were removed too.

facts.text: In late 1835 a small faction signed the Treaty of New Echota, giving up Cherokee land in the East; none were elected Cherokee officials, most Cherokee opposed it, and the Senate ratified it in 1836.
In 1838 US soldiers and state militia forced more than 16,000 Cherokee from their homes into camps and then west to Indian Territory, today's Oklahoma.
Elizur Butler, a missionary doctor who traveled with the Cherokee, estimated that over 4,000 died, nearly a fifth of the nation.
The Choctaw, Muscogee Creek, Seminole and Chickasaw were also relocated to Indian Territory in the 1830s.
After removal the Cherokee rebuilt their nation in Indian Territory, and the Cherokee Nation remains an independent tribe.

title: The Erie Canal
description: Finished in 1825, the canal linked the Great Lakes to New York City, opening the interior and making the city the leading commercial center.

facts.text: The Erie Canal, finished in 1825, linked the Great Lakes to New York City by way of the Hudson River at Albany.
The Erie Canal opened the interior of the continent to settlement and made New York City the nation's leading commercial center.

title: The Lowell mill girls
description: Young women from New England farms worked 12 to 14 hour days in Lowell’s mills for cash wages and struck in the turnouts of 1834 and 1836.

facts.text: Lowell's textile corporations recruited young women, generally 15 to 30, from New England farms with few other chances, offering monthly cash wages and board.
Most Lowell mill workers labored 12 to 14 hours a day and lived in company boardinghouses with curfews.
In 1834 and 1836 Lowell's women workers went on strike in turnouts against a wage cut and higher board charges.

title: Irish and German newcomers
description: The Great Famine (from 1845) sent Irish emigrants to Northeastern cities; Irish and German Catholics met nativist opposition, including the Know-Nothing party of the 1850s.

facts.text: Potato blight struck Ireland in 1845; about one million people died in the Great Famine, and perhaps 2 million more emigrated.
Most Irish immigrants settled in the cities where they landed, almost all in the Northeast.
All of the Irish and many German immigrants were Roman Catholic, which fed anti-Catholic opposition to them.
The anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic Know-Nothing party flourished in the 1850s; members were told to say they knew nothing about it.
The Know-Nothings wanted immigrants to wait far longer, 21 years, before they could become citizens.

title: The cotton gin
description: Whitney’s 1793 gin cleaned sticky-seeded inland cotton, making it profitable to grow across the South.

facts.text: Long-staple cotton, whose seeds come out easily, grew only near the coast; the cotton that grew inland had sticky seeds that were slow to pick out.
Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) pulled cotton fiber through wire teeth on a turning cylinder, leaving the seeds behind.

title: How cotton spread slavery
description: The gin did not cut the labor of planting and picking, so profitable cotton raised demand for land and enslaved people.

facts.text: The gin did not reduce the need for enslaved people to plant and pick cotton; cotton became so profitable that demand for land and enslaved labor grew.

title: The domestic slave trade
description: After the 1808 ban on imports from Africa, up to a million enslaved people were forced from the Upper South to the Deep South, splitting families.

facts.text: Congress banned the importation of enslaved people from Africa in 1808.
The domestic slave trade forced up to a million enslaved people from the Upper South to cotton plantations in the Deep South.
Enslaved people sold south were often marched in chained gangs, and sales separated spouses and families.

title: Family under slavery
description: The law did not recognize enslaved marriages and sales split families, but communities honored marriages, for example by jumping the broom.

facts.text: Southern laws refused to recognize marriages between enslaved people, and enslavers often separated spouses by sale.
Enslaved communities took marriage seriously; some couples jumped the broom, a ritual that validated marriages the law would not.

title: Faith in the hush harbors
description: Against obedience preaching, enslaved believers worshiped in secret hush harbors, blending African rhythms and beliefs with evangelical Christianity.

facts.text: Preachers approved by enslavers often taught that obedience to one's master was the highest religious duty.
Using signals and passwords whites could not read, enslaved believers called one another to secret worship in the woods, called hush harbors.
In their own worship, enslaved people mixed African rhythms, singing and beliefs with evangelical Christianity.

title: Spirituals
description: Religious folksongs made by enslaved people, passed on by ear in call and response, often with a double meaning of salvation and freedom.

facts.text: Spirituals were religious folksongs created by enslaved people in the South, passed on only by ear and sung in call and response.
Many spirituals carried double meanings: religious salvation, and freedom from slavery.

title: Everyday resistance and Nat Turner’s revolt
description: Enslaved people resisted by slowing work, feigning illness and breaking tools; Nat Turner’s 1831 revolt was followed by killings and harsher laws.

facts.text: Some enslaved people resisted every day by slowing down work, pretending to be sick or breaking tools.
In August 1831 in Southampton County, Virginia, Nat Turner led a revolt in which at least 55 white people were killed.
After Turner's revolt, whites killed at least 100 Black people, many uninvolved, and Turner was hanged.
Turner's revolt set off new laws banning the education, movement and assembly of enslaved people.

title: The Underground Railroad
description: Freedom seekers often escaped on their own; a secret network of stations and conductors grew to help them reach the North, Canada, Mexico and beyond.

facts.text: Many freedom seekers escaped on their own, without help; over time, helpers of all races built a secret network to assist them.
The Underground Railroad borrowed railway words: safe houses were stations and guides were conductors.
Freedom seekers headed not only north but to Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida and beyond.

title: Harriet Tubman
description: Tubman escaped in 1849 and made about 13 trips back to Maryland, never losing a passenger; older, larger counts are a legend.

facts.text: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 when she was about to be sold.
Tubman made about 13 trips back into Maryland to rescue family and friends, and later said she never lost a passenger.
An 1868 biography inflated Tubman's rescues to about 19 trips and 300 people; historians now accept about 13 trips.

title: Garrison and The Liberator
description: Garrison’s Liberator (1831) demanded immediate emancipation, and in 1833 he helped found the American Anti-Slavery Society.

facts.text: William Lloyd Garrison published the first issue of The Liberator on January 1, 1831, demanding immediate emancipation.
The first issue of The Liberator promised, in capital letters: "I WILL BE HEARD."
In 1833 Garrison helped organize the American Anti-Slavery Society.

title: Frederick Douglass, abolitionist
description: Douglass escaped in 1838, published his Narrative in 1845 to answer doubters, and started The North Star in 1847.

facts.text: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in September 1838 disguised as a sailor.
In 1845 Douglass published his Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, partly to answer those who doubted he had ever been enslaved.
In 1847 Douglass launched his own newspaper, The North Star, despite objections from Garrison and others.

title: Northern opposition to abolitionists
description: Many Northerners saw abolitionists as a threat to sectional harmony and the Constitution’s bargain; mobs killed Elijah Lovejoy in 1837.

facts.text: Many Northerners distrusted abolitionists, fearing they threatened harmony between North and South; immediate emancipation was unpopular even among many antislavery Northerners.
Abolitionists' critics argued that the Constitution left slavery to each state to decide.
Mobs destroyed Elijah Lovejoy's antislavery press several times, and on November 7, 1837, a mob in Alton, Illinois, killed him as he defended it.

title: Seneca Falls and its roots
description: Barred from the 1840 London antislavery convention, Mott and Stanton organized the 1848 Seneca Falls convention.

facts.text: At the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, women delegates were refused seats; Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton then agreed to hold a women's rights convention.
The first women's rights convention met at Seneca Falls, New York, on July 19 and 20, 1848.

title: The Declaration of Sentiments
description: Modeled on the Declaration of Independence (“all men and women are created equal”), it listed women’s legal grievances; its demand for the vote alone was not unanimous.

facts.text: Stanton's Declaration of Sentiments was modeled on the Declaration of Independence: "all men and women are created equal."
The Declaration of Sentiments said a married woman was, in the eye of the law, "civilly dead," with no right even to the wages she earned.
The resolution demanding women's right to the elective franchise, the vote, was the only one that did not pass unanimously.
Frederick Douglass spoke at Seneca Falls in support of women's rights.
In all, 100 people signed the Declaration of Sentiments: 68 women and 32 men.

title: Manifest Destiny
description: O’Sullivan’s 1845 phrase for the belief that the US had a God-given right to spread across the continent; Whigs called it arrogant.

facts.text: In 1845 the editor John L. O'Sullivan wrote of "our manifest destiny to overspread and to possess the whole of the continent."
Believers held that expanding to the Pacific was the nation's God-given right; Whigs attacked the idea as warlike and arrogant.

title: Texas, Oregon and the Mexican War
description: Texas joined in 1845 with a disputed border; Oregon was divided in 1846; war with Mexico (1846 to 1848) ended with Mexico ceding about 55 percent of its territory, while critics like Lincoln questioned the war.

facts.text: Texas won independence from Mexico in 1836 and joined the United States on December 29, 1845, but Mexico disputed its border: the Rio Grande or the Nueces River.
As settlers came on the Oregon Trail, an 1846 treaty with Britain divided the Oregon Country along the 49th parallel.
President James K. Polk sent troops into the disputed land, and after clashes there Congress declared war on Mexico on May 13, 1846.
In December 1847 Congressman Abraham Lincoln challenged Polk to show whether the spot where the war's first blood was shed was really US soil.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) ended the war; Mexico ceded about 55 percent of its territory, including California, for $15 million.

title: Mexicans in the ceded lands
description: The treaty promised Mexicans their property, but an 1851 law forced California landowners into costly title fights that often cost them the land.

facts.text: The treaty let Mexicans in the ceded lands stay and keep their property.
An 1851 law made Mexican landowners in California prove their titles, a slow, costly process; the cost was often the land itself.

title: The Missouri Compromise
description: In 1820 Missouri entered slave and Maine free, and slavery was barred north of 36°30′ in the Louisiana Territory.

facts.text: The Missouri Compromise (1820) admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, keeping the balance between them.
The Missouri Compromise banned slavery north of 36°30′ in the rest of the Louisiana Territory.

title: The Compromise of 1850
description: California entered free and New Mexico and Utah could decide, but the stricter Fugitive Slave Act turned many Northerners against slavery’s spread.

facts.text: The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state, let New Mexico and Utah territories decide on slavery, and ended the slave trade in Washington, DC.
Senator Henry Clay proposed the 1850 package, and Senator Stephen A. Douglas steered it through Congress.
The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required officials even in free states to arrest suspected freedom seekers and punished anyone who helped them escape.
The Fugitive Slave Act angered many in the North, turning moderate antislavery Northerners into firm opponents of slavery's spread.

title: The Kansas-Nebraska Act
description: In 1854 popular sovereignty replaced the Missouri line, and the rush of rival settlers produced Bleeding Kansas.

facts.text: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), sponsored by Douglas, let settlers decide slavery by popular sovereignty, repealing the Missouri Compromise line.
Proslavery and antislavery settlers rushed into Kansas, and the violence earned it the name Bleeding Kansas.

title: A house divided
description: In 1858 Lincoln argued the nation could not endure permanently half slave and half free, summing up how cotton, expansion and failed compromises split the country.

facts.text: On June 16, 1858, in Springfield, Illinois, Abraham Lincoln said: "A house divided against itself cannot stand."
Lincoln added: "I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free."

title: The Dred Scott decision
description: In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled that Black Americans were not citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

facts.text: Dred Scott, an enslaved man, sued for his freedom because he had lived in a free state and a free territory.
On March 6, 1857, Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not US citizens and could not sue in federal court.
The Dred Scott ruling said Congress had no power to ban slavery in the western territories.

title: From Harpers Ferry to secession
description: John Brown's raid and Lincoln's election led seven Deep South states to secede, and their own declarations named slavery as the reason.

facts.text: In October 1859, John Brown led a party of 22 raiders to seize the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to spark a revolt of enslaved people.
US Marines under Robert E. Lee captured Brown, and Virginia hanged him for treason on December 2, 1859.
Many Northerners hailed John Brown as a martyr, while many white Southerners saw his raid as proof of a Northern plot against the South.
In November 1860, Republican Abraham Lincoln, who opposed slavery's spread into the western territories, won the presidency without carrying a single slave state.
Lincoln said he had no purpose to interfere with slavery in the states where it already existed.
South Carolina seceded on December 20, 1860, and in February 1861 seven seceded states formed the Confederate States of America, with Jefferson Davis as president.
Mississippi's 1861 declaration of secession stated: "Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery."
Several seceding states issued declarations of causes that named the defense of slavery as their reason for leaving the Union.

title: Fort Sumter starts the war
description: The Confederate attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861 began the war; Lincoln's call for troops pushed four more states out.

facts.text: On April 12, 1861, Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, and Major Robert Anderson's outnumbered, undersupplied garrison surrendered.
No one was killed in the bombardment of Fort Sumter itself.
On April 15, 1861, Lincoln called for 75,000 militia to put down the rebellion.
After Lincoln's call for troops, Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee seceded, bringing the Confederacy to 11 states.

title: The border states
description: Four slave states stayed in the Union; their people, resources and routes made keeping them vital, which made Lincoln cautious about emancipation.

facts.text: Four slave states, Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri, stayed in the Union; they were called the border states.
The border states held large populations, farms and minerals, and key transportation routes; losing them would have badly weakened the Union.
In September 1861, Lincoln wrote: "I think to lose Kentucky is nearly the same as to lose the whole game."
Fear of pushing the loyal slave states toward the Confederacy made Lincoln cautious about freeing enslaved people early in the war.

title: Emancipation as a war measure
description: Lincoln framed emancipation as a war power to save the Union, issuing it after Antietam as a military necessity.

facts.text: In an August 22, 1862 letter to Horace Greeley, a New York editor, Lincoln wrote: "My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union."
When Lincoln wrote to Greeley, a draft of an emancipation proclamation was already on his desk.
After the Union victory at Antietam, Lincoln issued a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation on September 22, 1862.
Lincoln issued the Proclamation as commander in chief, calling it "a fit and necessary war measure for suppressing said rebellion."

title: What the Emancipation Proclamation did
description: From January 1, 1863, enslaved people in rebelling areas were declared free, with exemptions for loyal areas, and Black men could join the Union forces.

facts.text: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in areas in rebellion "are, and henceforward shall be free."
The Proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion; it left slavery untouched in the loyal border states and in Confederate areas the Union already held.
After January 1, 1863, every advance of Union troops widened the area where enslaved people were legally free.
The Emancipation Proclamation announced that Black men would be accepted into the Union Army and Navy.

title: Self-emancipation
description: Enslaved people who escaped to Union lines, starting at Fort Monroe in 1861, forced the question of freedom; historians debate how to weigh their role and Lincoln's.

facts.text: In May 1861, Frank Baker, Shepard Mallory and James Townsend escaped slavery and rowed a small boat to Fort Monroe, a Union fort in Virginia.
General Benjamin Butler refused to return them, declaring people who fled to Union lines "contraband of war."
Within months, hundreds more enslaved people had fled to Fort Monroe.
On June 2, 1863, Harriet Tubman helped lead a Union raid up the Combahee River in South Carolina that freed more than 700 enslaved people.
Historian Ira Berlin argued that enslaved people were the prime movers of their own emancipation; James McPherson argued Lincoln's role was decisive.
Much recent scholarship shows self-emancipation working together with military emancipation and laws passed by Congress.

title: Black soldiers in the Union forces
description: About 179,000 Black men served in the Union Army, fighting at places like Fort Wagner despite unequal pay until 1864.

facts.text: About 179,000 Black men served in the Union Army, 10 percent of it, and about 19,000 more served in the Navy.
Black soldiers were first paid $10 a month minus $3 for clothing, while white privates got $13; Congress granted equal pay in June 1864.
In July 1863 the 54th Massachusetts led an assault on Fort Wagner, South Carolina; about 272 of its roughly 650 men were killed, wounded or captured.

title: Gettysburg and Vicksburg
description: In July 1863 the Union stopped Lee's invasion at Gettysburg and took Vicksburg, splitting the Confederacy along the Mississippi.

facts.text: The Battle of Gettysburg, fought in Pennsylvania from July 1 to 3, 1863, ended Robert E. Lee's second invasion of the North.
As many as 51,000 soldiers from both armies were killed, wounded, captured or missing at Gettysburg, the war's bloodiest battle.
On July 3, 1863, about 15,000 Confederates attacked the Union center in Pickett's Charge; the assault failed, and Lee retreated to Virginia.
Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy.

title: The Gettysburg Address
description: Lincoln's short speech of November 1863 tied the war to 1776's promise of equality and a "new birth of freedom."

facts.text: On November 19, 1863, Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of a cemetery for Union soldiers killed in the battle.
The Gettysburg Address is roughly 270 words long.
The address opens "Four score and seven years ago," 87 years before 1863, pointing to 1776 and the proposition "that all men are created equal."
Lincoln closed by resolving that the nation "shall have a new birth of freedom" and that government "of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth."

title: Sherman's hard war
description: Sherman took Atlanta and marched to the sea in 1864, destroying railroads and supplies to break the South's ability to fight.

facts.text: Union general William T. Sherman captured Atlanta on September 2, 1864, a victory that helped Lincoln win reelection that November.
From November 15 to December 21, 1864, Sherman's army marched about 285 miles from Atlanta to Savannah, living off the land and destroying railroads and supplies.
Sherman aimed to wreck the Confederacy's ability to make war and to bring the war home to Southern civilians.

title: Drafts and riots on the home fronts
description: Both sides drafted soldiers, the rich could buy their way out, and anger boiled over in New York's draft riots and Richmond's bread riot.

facts.text: The Confederacy passed the first national draft in American history in April 1862.
The Union's Enrollment Act of March 3, 1863, let a drafted man hire a substitute or pay $300 to avoid service.
Critics called the conflict "a rich man's war but a poor man's fight."
In July 1863, New York City draft rioters attacked Black residents and burned the Colored Orphan Asylum; more than 100 people were killed.
On April 2, 1863, women in Richmond, the Confederate capital, many of them soldiers' wives, rioted over food prices, crying "Bread or blood!"
Dorothea Dix became superintendent of women nurses for the Union Army in 1861, and thousands of women served as nurses.

title: How the war ended
description: Lincoln called for peace without malice; Lee surrendered at Appomattox on April 9, 1865, after a war that killed 620,000 to 750,000.

facts.text: In his second inaugural address on March 4, 1865, Lincoln urged the nation on "with malice toward none, with charity for all."
In the same address, Lincoln said that slavery was "somehow the cause of the war."
Robert E. Lee surrendered his army to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, on April 9, 1865.
Grant's terms let Confederate soldiers go home on parole, and those who owned horses or mules could keep them for farming.
About 620,000 soldiers died by the long-accepted count; a 2011 census-based study by J. David Hacker estimated about 750,000.

title: Lincoln's assassination
description: Booth killed Lincoln in April 1865, putting Andrew Johnson and his lenient terms for the South in charge of Reconstruction.

facts.text: John Wilkes Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in Washington on April 14, 1865; Lincoln died the next morning.
Vice President Andrew Johnson, a Southerner who had opposed secession, was sworn in as president on April 15, 1865.
Johnson pardoned most white Southerners and let former Confederate states rebuild their governments with little federal oversight.
Many Republicans in Congress were outraged by Johnson's pardons, as Southern states sent former Confederate leaders to Congress.

title: The 13th and 14th Amendments
description: The 13th Amendment ended slavery (except as punishment for crime); the 14th made everyone born here a citizen with equal protection, undoing Dred Scott.

facts.text: The 13th Amendment bans slavery and involuntary servitude "except as a punishment for crime."
The 14th Amendment, ratified July 9, 1868, made "all persons born or naturalized in the United States" citizens.
The 14th Amendment bars states from denying any person "due process of law" or "the equal protection of the laws."
Congress wrote the 14th Amendment's citizenship clause to undo the Dred Scott decision.
Historian Eric Foner calls the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments a "second founding" because they remade the Constitution.

title: The 15th Amendment
description: The 15th Amendment (1870) barred race discrimination in voting but left out women, splitting the women's rights movement.

facts.text: The 15th Amendment, ratified February 3, 1870, bars denying the vote "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude."
