Because the 15th Amendment did not cover women, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed it, while Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass supported it.

title: What Reconstruction achieved
description: The Freedmen's Bureau built schools and Black men voted and won office, including the first Black senator and representative in 1870.

facts.text: Congress created the Freedmen's Bureau on March 3, 1865; it set up schools, oversaw labor contracts and helped freedpeople reunite with family.
Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first African American US senator in 1870.
Joseph Rainey of South Carolina, born enslaved, became the first African American in the US House on December 12, 1870.

title: How Reconstruction ended
description: Klan terror and massacres like Colfax attacked Black voters, and after the disputed 1876 election federal troops left the South in 1877.

facts.text: Confederate veterans founded the Ku Klux Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865 or 1866; it used terror against Black Americans to undo Reconstruction.
On April 13, 1873, armed white men attacked Black defenders of the courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana; estimates of the Black dead run as high as about 150.
After the disputed 1876 election, Democrats accepted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes as president, and in 1877 he withdrew the last federal troops protecting Southern Republican governments.
Historian C. Vann Woodward (1951) argued a secret bargain settled the 1876 election; Allan Peskin (1973) questioned whether it was a true compromise.

title: Civil War and Reconstruction: freedom won, equality lost
description: Between 1865 and 1877 the nation ended slavery and wrote citizenship and voting rights into the Constitution, then withdrew the federal protection of those rights.

facts.text: Between 1865 and 1877, the US abolished slavery and wrote citizenship and voting rights into the Constitution, then withdrew federal troops from the South.

title: The transcontinental railroad
description: Two companies, largely Chinese immigrant labor on the Central Pacific, joined the coasts by rail in 1869.

facts.text: In 1862 Congress passed the first Pacific Railroad Act to build a railroad across the continent.
The Union Pacific built west from Nebraska while the Central Pacific built east from California.
The two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869.
Chinese immigrants made up about 90 percent of the Central Pacific’s workforce by the end of construction.

title: The Homestead Act
description: The 1862 act offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and farmed it.

facts.text: Lincoln signed the Homestead Act of 1862, which offered 160 acres of public land for a filing fee to settlers who lived on and farmed it.
Homesteaders included immigrants, farmers without land of their own, single women and formerly enslaved people.

title: The bison slaughter
description: Railways, hide hunters and the army nearly wiped out the bison the Plains nations depended on.

facts.text: Bison fell from an estimated 30 to 60 million to fewer than 1,000 animals by the 1890s.
Railways, rifles and an international market for hides drove the ’Great Slaughter’ of bison from about 1820 to 1880.
The US military encouraged destroying the bison as a way to control Native nations who depended on them.

title: The fight over the Black Hills
description: The US recognized the Black Hills as Sioux land in 1868, then took them after gold was found.

facts.text: In the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868, the US recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation.
In 1874 George Armstrong Custer led an expedition into the Black Hills; gold was found, and miners poured in.
The government ordered the Lakota to return to reservations by January 31, 1876, or be treated as hostile.
In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled the Black Hills had been taken and payment was owed; the Sioux refused the money, seeking the land.

title: The Little Bighorn
description: Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters defeated Custer in 1876, a victory followed by forced surrender.

facts.text: On June 25, 1876, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Custer at the Little Bighorn.
Custer and every soldier who followed him into the battle were killed.
After the battle, the army flooded the region and forced the Lakota and their allies to surrender.
The Lakota and Cheyenne were Plains nations, living on the Great Plains.

title: Wounded Knee
description: In 1890 the 7th Cavalry killed hundreds of Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek after the Ghost Dance alarmed officials.

facts.text: By 1890, facing hunger and a shrinking reservation, some Lakota turned to the Ghost Dance, which alarmed some US officials.
On December 29, 1890, the 7th Cavalry killed about 150 to 300 Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, almost half of them women and children.

title: Indian boarding schools
description: Government boarding schools such as Carlisle tried to strip Native children of their languages and cultures.

facts.text: In 1879, army officer Richard Henry Pratt opened a boarding school for Native children in Carlisle, Pennsylvania.
Pratt described his aim as to ’kill the Indian in him, and save the man.’
Boarding schools separated children from their families, cut their hair, changed their names and dress, and forbade their own languages.
Zitkála-Šá, a Yankton Dakota writer sent to a boarding school at 8, exposed its harms in Atlantic Monthly essays in 1900.
In 1926 Zitkála-Šá and her husband founded the National Council of American Indians.

title: The Dawes Act and allotment
description: Allotment split reservations into individual plots and sold the rest, cutting Native land by about two-thirds.

facts.text: The Dawes Act of 1887 split reservation land held in common into individual allotments, a quarter section (160 acres) per head of family.
Reservation land left over after allotment was declared ’surplus’ and could be sold to non-Native settlers.
The act’s backers expected that owning a farm would lead Native people to drop their own cultures and assimilate.
Native nations held about 138 million acres before the Dawes Act and only about 48 million by 1934.
The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended allotment.

title: Why the Gilded Age
description: The era is named after an 1873 novel: gilded means gold on the surface only.

facts.text: The Gilded Age is named after an 1873 novel by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner; ’gilded’ means thinly covered in gold.

title: Carnegie and steel
description: A Scottish immigrant bobbin boy built a steel empire, sold it for $480 million and preached the Gospel of Wealth.

facts.text: Andrew Carnegie’s family emigrated from Scotland to Pittsburgh in 1848, and at 13 he worked as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill.
In 1901 Carnegie sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan for $480 million.
In 1889 Carnegie argued that the rich have a duty to use their surplus wealth for the improvement of mankind: the Gospel of Wealth.

title: Rockefeller and Standard Oil
description: Standard Oil came to refine 90 to 95 percent of US oil by buying rivals and using railroad rebates.

facts.text: John D. Rockefeller’s Standard Oil Company was incorporated in Ohio in 1870.
By 1880, by buying out rivals, merging and using railroad rebates, Standard Oil refined 90 to 95 percent of US oil.

title: Robber barons or industrial statesmen?
description: Historians such as Josephson and Nevins read the same record as plunder or as order-building.

facts.text: In his 1934 book The Robber Barons, Matthew Josephson cast the industrialists as unscrupulous pirates grabbing the economy.
In a 1940 Rockefeller biography, Allan Nevins argued he brought order to a chaotic industry, despite unethical tactics.

title: Workers organize and strike
description: Workers formed unions to bargain as a group, and strikes like Homestead (1892) and the 1909 Uprising tested their power.

facts.text: A labor union is an association of workers that seeks better pay and conditions by bargaining with employers as a group.
In 1892, at Carnegie’s Homestead steel works, managers locked out workers and sent 300 Pinkerton agents to seize the plant.
The battle at Homestead left three Pinkertons and seven strikers dead; the state militia then broke the strike and the union.
In November 1909, Clara Lemlich, 23, called for a general strike, and thousands of shirtwaist makers walked out.
The strikers were mostly young immigrant women; the Uprising of the 20,000 lasted over two months and won better pay and shorter hours at many shops.

title: The Triangle fire
description: The 1911 fire killed 146 workers behind locked doors and led New York to pass new safety laws.

facts.text: On March 25, 1911, a fire at the Triangle Waist Company in New York killed 146 garment workers, mostly young immigrant women.
The factory doors were locked or opened inward, and many exits were blocked or broken.
New York’s Factory Investigating Commission led to more than 30 health and safety laws, including fire codes and child labor limits.
Frances Perkins witnessed the fire and later became US Secretary of Labor.

title: The new immigrants and Ellis Island
description: From 1880 to 1920 millions came from southern and eastern Europe, most through Ellis Island.

facts.text: Between 1880 and 1920, a great wave of immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe.
Between 1881 and 1924, over 2.5 million eastern European Jews came to the US, driven by persecution and poverty.
Ellis Island opened in 1892, and more than 12 million immigrants passed through it by 1924.
Only about 2 percent of arrivals at Ellis Island were refused entry, most often for contagious disease.

title: Chinese exclusion and Angel Island
description: The 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act singled out one nationality; Angel Island held Asian immigrants for weeks or months.

facts.text: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred Chinese laborers: the first major US law to suspend immigration of one nationality.
Congress repealed the Chinese exclusion laws in 1943, when China was a World War II ally.
Angel Island Immigration Station in San Francisco Bay opened in 1910, the main western entry point for immigrants from Asia.
Chinese and Japanese immigrants were often held at Angel Island for weeks or months while officials checked their papers.
Chinese detainees carved poems into the barracks walls, expressing frustration and sorrow over their detention.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
description: A planned challenge to Louisiana’s train law led the Supreme Court to approve "separate but equal" in 1896.

facts.text: Louisiana’s Separate Car Act of 1890 required separate railway cars for Black and white passengers.
In 1892, Homer Plessy, recruited by New Orleans’ Comité des Citoyens to test the law, sat in a whites-only car.
In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 1 that segregation was constitutional if facilities were ’equal.’
Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented, writing: ’Our Constitution is color-blind.’

title: Taking away the vote
description: Poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses shut Black men out of voting across the former Confederacy.

facts.text: Southern states used poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses to keep Black men from voting.
From Mississippi in 1890 to Georgia in 1908, every former Confederate state moved to disfranchise Black voters.

title: Ida B. Wells against lynching
description: Wells investigated lynchings, exposed their false excuses and helped found the NAACP.

facts.text: In 1892 a Memphis mob lynched Ida B. Wells’s friend Thomas Moss and two other Black grocers who competed with a white-owned store.
Wells investigated lynchings and found the usual excuse for them was almost always false; a mob destroyed her newspaper’s office.
Wells published her findings in the 1892 pamphlet Southern Horrors.
In 1909 Wells took part in the conference that founded the NAACP.

title: Muckrakers and monopoly
description: Reporters like Ida Tarbell exposed Standard Oil, which the Supreme Court broke up in 1911.

facts.text: Ida Tarbell’s History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), serialized in McClure’s, exposed its unfair tactics and railroad rebates.
In 1911 the Supreme Court ruled Standard Oil had broken the Sherman Antitrust Act and ordered it split into 34 companies.

title: The Jungle and food safety
description: Sinclair’s The Jungle helped win the 1906 meat and food laws.

facts.text: Upton Sinclair’s novel The Jungle (1906) exposed filthy, dangerous conditions in Chicago’s meatpacking plants.
Public outrage helped pass the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act, both in 1906.

title: City machines and reformers
description: Tweed’s Tammany ring looted New York; reformers like Jane Addams built help for immigrant neighborhoods.

facts.text: Boss William Tweed’s Tammany Hall ring plundered New York City of an estimated $30 million to $200 million.
Thomas Nast’s cartoons helped expose the Tweed Ring, and Tweed was convicted in 1873.
In 1889 Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull-House in Chicago, offering immigrant neighbors classes, childcare and job help.

title: The West votes first
description: Women won the vote first in western territories and states, starting with Wyoming in 1869.

facts.text: On December 10, 1869, Wyoming Territory became the first in the US to grant women the vote.
Women of the West were the first in the US to win full voting rights, state by state and territory by territory.

title: Winning the 19th Amendment
description: Catt’s Winning Plan and Paul’s pickets pushed the 19th Amendment to ratification in August 1920.

facts.text: In 1916 Carrie Chapman Catt’s ’Winning Plan’ paired promising state campaigns with lobbying for a federal amendment.
From January 1917, Alice Paul’s ’Silent Sentinels’ picketed the White House, and many were arrested.
Sentenced to seven months in jail, Alice Paul led a hunger strike in protest.
On August 18, 1920, Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment, after Harry Burn cast the deciding vote.
Burn said he changed his vote after a letter from his mother urging him to support suffrage.

title: Who the 19th Amendment left out
description: Black women in the South and many Native women still could not vote after 1920.

facts.text: In the South, Black women who tried to register after 1920 faced poll taxes, literacy tests and violence.
Many Native American women could not vote in 1920 because they were not recognized as citizens until 1924.

title: An urban nation
description: By 1920, rails, factories and immigration had made the US a nation where most people lived in urban areas.

facts.text: The 1920 census was the first in which most Americans lived in urban areas.

title: The war with Spain
description: How the 1898 war over Cuba left the US with colonies in the Caribbean and the Pacific.

facts.text: From 1895 to 1898 Cuban revolutionaries fought for independence from Spain, and many Americans sympathized with them.
The US battleship Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbor on February 15, 1898.
The US declared war on Spain on April 25, 1898, and in the Teller Amendment Congress pledged not to annex Cuba.
In the Treaty of Paris, signed December 10, 1898, Spain ceded Puerto Rico and Guam and sold the Philippines to the US for $20 million.
In 1893 planters and businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Hawaii's Queen Liliuokalani; the US annexed Hawaii in 1898.
In 1897 more than 21,000 Native Hawaiians signed petitions against annexation, and the annexation treaty failed in the Senate.

title: Empire debated
description: How Filipinos fought for independence and how imperialists and anti-imperialists argued over annexation.

facts.text: Filipino revolutionaries led by Emilio Aguinaldo proclaimed an independent Philippine Republic; they wanted independence, not new rulers.
The Philippine-American War (1899 to 1902) killed over 4,200 US and over 20,000 Filipino soldiers; up to 200,000 Filipino civilians died.
Annexation backers wanted Asian trade, doubted Filipinos could govern themselves, and feared Germany or Japan would take the islands.
The Anti-Imperialist League, formed in 1898 to fight annexing the Philippines, included Andrew Carnegie, Mark Twain and Samuel Gompers.
The league's 1899 platform declared that "governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed."

title: From neutrality to war
description: How submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram moved the US from neutrality to war in 1917.

facts.text: When war broke out in Europe in 1914, Wilson declared the US neutral; he was reelected in 1916 on the slogan "He kept us out of war."
A German submarine sank the British liner Lusitania on May 7, 1915, killing 128 Americans; Wilson still kept the US out of the war.
On February 1, 1917, Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, attacking Allied and neutral ships in war zones.
The Zimmermann Telegram proposed that Mexico ally with Germany and "reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona."
Wilson asked Congress for war on April 2, 1917, and Congress declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917.

title: Arguing over war
description: What Wilson and his opponents in Congress argued about joining World War I.

facts.text: In his war message, Wilson declared: "The world must be made safe for democracy."
By 1917 American bankers had loaned the Allies over $2 billion.
House opponents argued no vital interest was threatened, the public didn't want war, and arms makers and business interests were pushing it.
The House voted 373 to 50 for war; Jeannette Rankin, the first woman in Congress, told the House: "I cannot vote for war."

title: Americans in the fight
description: How American troops, including Black and Native soldiers, fought in France in 1918.

facts.text: The Meuse-Argonne Offensive, from September 26 to November 11, 1918, was the AEF's largest operation, with over a million US soldiers.
The fighting ended with an armistice on November 11, 1918.
The 369th Infantry, a Black regiment called the Harlem Hellfighters, spent 191 days in front-line trenches, more than any US unit its size.
In France in 1918, Choctaw soldiers became the first Code Talkers, sending battle messages in Choctaw that the enemy never broke.

title: The Great Migration
description: Why millions of Black Southerners moved north and west, and what they found there.

facts.text: From the 1910s to the 1970s, about six million Black Southerners moved north and west, one of the largest migrations in US history.
Migrants left to escape racial violence and the oppression of Jim Crow, and to find better jobs and schooling.
From 1917, men leaving for the war and a drop in immigration from Europe opened industrial jobs to Black workers.
Migrants settled in cities such as New York, Chicago and Detroit.
In the North, migrants still met discrimination, including in housing, and racial violence in the Red Summer of 1919.

title: The Harlem Renaissance
description: How Black writers and musicians in Harlem, such as Langston Hughes, celebrated African American culture.

facts.text: Langston Hughes, whose first book of poems, The Weary Blues, appeared in 1926, became a leading writer of the Harlem Renaissance.
The Harlem Renaissance celebrated African American culture and achievement.
Hughes said the people he met in everyday life inspired his work, and blues and jazz gave it its rhythm.

title: Prohibition
description: Why temperance reformers won a national ban on alcohol, and what the ban produced.

facts.text: From the 1870s the Women's Christian Temperance Union saw alcohol as the source of many social ills, including ruined families.
The 18th Amendment banned the "manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors" for beverage purposes.
National Prohibition began in January 1920.
Illegal liquor stayed easy to find, and gangsters like Al Capone grew rich from bootlegging while bribing police, judges and politicians.

title: Repeal
description: Why Americans, led in part by women's groups, repealed Prohibition in 1933.

facts.text: In 1929 Pauline Sabin founded the Women's Organization for National Prohibition Reform, which grew to 1.5 million reported members.
Repeal women argued Prohibition had led to more unregulated and underage drinking and to distrust of the law.
After the 1929 crash, the promise of jobs and tax revenue from legal alcohol built support for repeal.
The 21st Amendment, ratified December 5, 1933, repealed the 18th Amendment and ended national Prohibition.

title: Living through the Depression
description: How ordinary Americans lived through the crash, joblessness and forced removals of the 1930s.

facts.text: On Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, the stock market fell nearly 12 percent; by mid-November it had lost almost half its value.
At the Depression's worst, in 1933, about a quarter of the workforce (24.9 percent) had no job.
Homeless families built shantytowns from packing crates and scrap, nicknamed "Hoovervilles."
In the 1930s officials pushed Mexicans and Mexican Americans, many US-born citizens, to Mexico; estimates range from 400,000 to 2 million.

title: The Dust Bowl
description: Why drought and farming practices turned the southern Plains into the Dust Bowl and drove families west.

facts.text: Repeated droughts struck Plains farms that had spread onto poorer land and cut back on soil conservation, leaving soil to blow away.
On Black Sunday, April 14, 1935, a wall of dust turned a sunny afternoon darker than night across the southern Plains.
An Associated Press reporter, Robert Geiger, coined the term Dust Bowl in 1935.
Many Plains families, called "Okies," abandoned their farms and headed to California in search of work.

title: The New Deal's programs
description: What the New Deal built, from the CCC to Social Security.

facts.text: In his first inaugural address, on March 4, 1933, FDR said "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself."
New Deal agencies such as the CCC (1933) and the WPA put unemployed Americans to work on conservation, construction and arts projects.
By 1942, over 2.5 million men had served in the Civilian Conservation Corps.
The Social Security Act, signed August 14, 1935, created old-age benefits and unemployment insurance.

title: Who the New Deal left out
description: How Social Security's exclusions left out most Black workers, and how historians explain them.

facts.text: The act left out agricultural workers and domestic servants in private homes.
About 65 percent of African Americans were left out of the new benefits.
In 1935 the NAACP's Charles Hamilton Houston warned Congress the exemptions would leave out Black sharecroppers and tenants.
Social Security historian Larry DeWitt argues the exclusions came from the practical problem of collecting taxes, not racial motives.

title: Critics left and right
description: Why some critics said the New Deal went too far and others said it did not go far enough.

facts.text: Senator Huey Long pushed his Share Our Wealth plan to spread wealth; by spring 1935 over seven million Americans had joined its societies.
The American Liberty League, founded in 1934 by business leaders and politicians, attacked the New Deal as unconstitutional.

title: Staying out
description: Why Congress passed Neutrality Acts in the 1930s.

facts.text: In the 1930s, Senator Gerald Nye's report claimed bankers and arms makers had pushed the US into World War I for their own profit.
The first Neutrality Act, passed August 31, 1935, banned exporting "arms, ammunition, and implements of war" to nations at war.

title: Aiding Britain
description: How the US moved from cash and carry to Lend-Lease, and who opposed it.

facts.text: In November 1939 a new Neutrality Act let nations at war buy arms from the US on a "cash and carry" basis.
In 1940 FDR won a third term, breaking the two-term tradition set by George Washington.
Under Lend-Lease, passed in March 1941, the US supplied Britain with war materials without demanding immediate payment.
Many Americans opposed another war, and Army chief George Marshall argued supplies should be saved to defend the Western Hemisphere.

title: Why Japan attacked
description: How the US embargo on Japan led to the attack on Pearl Harbor and war on two fronts.

facts.text: As Japan pushed into China and Indochina, the US froze Japanese assets and imposed a full embargo on exports to Japan, including oil.
The attack on Pearl Harbor killed more than 2,400 Americans.
The day after the attack the US declared war on Japan; when Germany then declared war on the US, it faced war in Europe and Asia.

title: Winning the war
description: How the US fought on two fronts, from Midway and D-Day to Japan's surrender.

facts.text: At Midway, June 4 to 7, 1942, US code breakers uncovered Japan's plan and Japan lost four aircraft carriers, turning the Pacific war.
On D-Day, June 6, 1944, nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed in Normandy, France; Americans came ashore at Utah and Omaha beaches.
Germany surrendered in May 1945.
Japan formally surrendered aboard USS Missouri on September 2, 1945, ending World War II.
The Marines trained over 400 Navajo men as Code Talkers, many serving in the Pacific, and the Japanese never broke their code.
The US military grew from about 334,000 people in 1939 to over 12 million in 1945.

title: The atomic bomb debate
description: What happened at Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and how historians disagree about the decision.

facts.text: The US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9, 1945; the next day Japan's emperor pushed to surrender.
Historians called traditionalists argue the bombs were necessary to save American lives and prevent a US invasion of Japan.
Revisionists such as Gar Alperovitz argue the bombs were unnecessary since Japan was near surrender, and partly aimed at the Soviets.

title: New work, new demands
description: How the war opened jobs to women and how Black Americans pressed for equal treatment.

facts.text: More than six million women took wartime factory jobs; Rosie the Riveter became their symbol.
Labor leader A. Philip Randolph threatened to bring tens of thousands of Black marchers to Washington unless defense jobs opened to them.
Executive Order 8802, issued June 25, 1941, declared "There shall be no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries."
In 1942 the Pittsburgh Courier, a Black newspaper, launched the Double V campaign: victory over fascism abroad and racism at home.

title: Japanese American incarceration
description: Why Japanese Americans were forced into camps, and how the country later apologized.

facts.text: Executive Order 9066, issued February 19, 1942, led to the forced removal of about 122,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
Nearly 70,000 of them were US citizens; none were charged with a crime, and they had no way to appeal.
The government called the guarded camps "relocation centers"; they were also known as "internment camps."
Gordon Hirabayashi and Fred Korematsu challenged the orders in court, but the Supreme Court upheld them.
More than 30,000 Japanese Americans served in World War II, in segregated units.
In 1988 Congress apologized for the incarceration and paid $20,000 to each person who had been held.

title: A world power with a bigger government
description: How war, boom and depression between 1898 and 1945 made the US a world power with a much larger federal government.

facts.text: Before the Great Depression, federal spending was less than 3 percent of GDP; by 1939 federal outlays exceeded 10 percent.

title: Containment
description: After 1947 the US tried to contain Soviet expansion by aiding threatened countries, from the Truman Doctrine on.

facts.text: In March 1947 President Harry Truman asked Congress for $400 million in aid to Greece and Turkey.
The Truman Doctrine made it US policy “to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.”
In a 1947 article, diplomat George Kennan called for “patient but firm and vigilant containment” of Soviet expansion.

title: Korea and the arms race
description: The Korean War (1950 to 1953) and the Soviet bomb of 1949 turned the Cold War hot abroad and nuclear.

facts.text: On June 25, 1950, North Korea invaded South Korea, and United Nations forces fought to defend the South.
An armistice on July 27, 1953, stopped the fighting and left Korea divided near the 38th parallel, with no peace treaty.
The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in August 1949, ending the US monopoly on nuclear weapons.
The US tested the first hydrogen bomb, far more powerful than an atomic bomb, in 1952, and a nuclear arms race followed.

title: The Red Scare
description: McCarthy’s accusations came with little proof, while Soviet espionage was nonetheless real.

facts.text: On February 9, 1950, in Wheeling, West Virginia, Senator Joseph McCarthy claimed to have a list of Communists in the State Department.
McCarthy offered little proof for his accusations, and on December 2, 1954, the Senate voted to censure him.
Decoded Soviet cables released in 1995, the Venona project, confirmed that Soviet spies had worked inside the US government.

title: The GI Bill
description: The 1944 GI Bill paid for veterans’ education and helped them buy homes.

facts.text: President Franklin Roosevelt signed the GI Bill (Servicemen’s Readjustment Act) on June 22, 1944, days after D-Day.
The GI Bill gave World War II veterans money for college, unemployment pay and help buying homes.
Within seven years, about eight million veterans had used the GI Bill’s education benefits.

title: Levittown and the interstates
description: Mass-built houses and federal highways made the postwar suburbs.

facts.text: Between 1947 and 1951, Levitt & Sons mass-produced more than 17,000 houses at Levittown on Long Island, New York.
The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, signed by President Dwight Eisenhower, funded about 41,000 miles of interstate highways.

title: Shut out of the suburbs
description: Covenants and FHA redlining kept most Black families, veterans included, out of new suburbs.

facts.text: Every Levittown sales contract barred buyers who were “not member(s) of the Caucasian race.”
The Federal Housing Administration largely refused to insure mortgages in Black neighborhoods and steered lenders toward segregated ones.
Black veterans were often unable to get GI Bill home loans, and were largely kept out of new white suburbs.

title: The NAACP legal campaign
description: Thurgood Marshall and NAACP lawyers chipped at segregation case by case, starting with graduate schools.

facts.text: In the 1930s and 1940s, NAACP lawyers first attacked segregation in graduate and law schools, where states rarely had separate Black schools.
Sweatt v. Painter (1950), a win against a segregated Texas law school, was a major test case in Thurgood Marshall’s strategy.

title: Brown v. Board
description: In 1954 a unanimous Court ruled segregated schools inherently unequal.

facts.text: Brown v. Board of Education combined five lawsuits from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and Washington, D.C.
On May 17, 1954, a unanimous Supreme Court ruled that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,” violating equal protection.
Thurgood Marshall, the NAACP’s lead counsel in Brown, later became a Supreme Court justice himself.

title: Little Rock and resistance
description: Brown II’s vague timetable and Southern resistance slowed integration, as at Little Rock in 1957.

facts.text: In Brown II (1955), the Court told states to desegregate “with all deliberate speed,” a vague phrase many districts used to delay.
In September 1957, Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock’s Central High.
President Eisenhower federalized the Arkansas Guard and sent the 101st Airborne; the Nine entered Central High under escort on September 25, 1957.

title: The sit-ins
description: The Greensboro sit-in of 1960 spread across the South and led to SNCC.

facts.text: On February 1, 1960, four Black students from North Carolina A&T sat at the whites-only Woolworth’s lunch counter in Greensboro.
By the end of March 1960, nonviolent sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states.
In April 1960, organizer Ella Baker brought sit-in leaders to Raleigh, where they founded the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC).
Part of the Greensboro Woolworth’s lunch counter is now displayed at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.

title: The Freedom Rides
description: CORE’s 1961 Freedom Riders tested an unenforced ruling until the federal government acted.

facts.text: In Boynton v. Virginia (1960), the Supreme Court banned segregation in bus stations serving interstate travelers, but it went unenforced.
In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) sent interracial Freedom Riders south on buses to test the ruling.
On May 14, 1961, near Anniston, Alabama, a mob set a Freedom Riders’ bus on fire with the riders aboard.
In September 1961 the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered interstate buses and terminals desegregated.

title: The March on Washington
description: The 1963 march drew about 250,000 people, and the Civil Rights Act followed in 1964.

facts.text: On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, planned by A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin.
At the March on Washington, Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech.
On July 2, 1964, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, banning segregation in public places.

title: The Sputnik shock
description: Sputnik in 1957 made Americans fear they had fallen behind, and Congress created NASA and funded science education.

facts.text: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, which sent out a beeping radio signal.
Sputnik fed fears that the US had fallen behind in technology; the Soviets had also tested the first intercontinental ballistic missile that year.
On July 29, 1958, President Eisenhower signed the law creating NASA.
The National Defense Education Act of 1958 funded schools and colleges so the US could compete with the Soviets in science.

title: Racing to the Moon
description: After Gagarin’s flight, Kennedy set the Moon goal that Apollo 11 met in 1969, amid debate over its cost.

facts.text: On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On May 25, 1961, President John F. Kennedy asked Congress to commit to landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out.
Katherine Johnson, a Black NASA mathematician, calculated trajectories for the Apollo 11 mission.
Apollo 11’s Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above.
As Apollo 11 prepared to launch, Ralph Abernathy led a Poor People’s Campaign protest, with mules and a wagon, to the Kennedy Space Center.

title: Why the US fought in Vietnam
description: The domino theory and the Tonkin Resolution drew the US into a war that peaked above half a million troops.

facts.text: In April 1954 President Eisenhower warned that if Indochina fell to communism, its neighbors could fall like dominoes.
In August 1964 Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, letting President Johnson use force; the House voted 414 to 0, the Senate 88 to 2.
By 1968 the US had more than half a million troops in Vietnam.
The Tet Offensive of January 1968 failed militarily, but its size shook Americans who had been told the war was nearly won.

title: Vietnam divides the nation
description: The draft, protest, Kent State and the silent majority split Americans until US withdrawal in 1973.

facts.text: More than 58,000 Americans died in the Vietnam War.
College deferments let many better-off young men avoid the draft, so most draftees came from poor and working-class families.
On November 3, 1969, President Richard Nixon asked the “great silent majority” of Americans to support his war policy against protesters.
On May 4, 1970, Ohio National Guardsmen fired on antiwar protesters at Kent State University, killing four students.
The Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 brought a ceasefire and the withdrawal of US forces.
Fighting went on, and on April 30, 1975, Saigon, South Vietnam’s capital, fell to North Vietnam.

title: Title IX
description: Title IX (1972) barred sex discrimination in federally funded education.

facts.text: Title IX (1972) says no person shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from any education program receiving federal money.
President Richard Nixon signed Title IX into law on June 23, 1972.

title: Farmworkers organize
description: Filipino and Mexican American farmworkers struck and boycotted grapes, winning contracts in 1970.

facts.text: In September 1965, Filipino American grape workers led by Larry Itliong went on strike in Delano, California.
Itliong persuaded César Chávez and Dolores Huerta’s mostly Mexican American union to join; in 1967 the unions merged into the United Farm Workers.
After a national grape boycott, growers signed contracts in 1970 promising farmworkers better pay and benefits.

title: Native self-determination
description: Alcatraz activism and federal policy shifted toward tribal self-government by 1975.

facts.text: In November 1969, Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island, citing an 1868 treaty, and held it for 19 months.
In July 1970, President Nixon called for “self-determination without termination” for Native nations.
The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act of 1975 let tribal governments run their own federal programs.

title: The ERA debate
description: The ERA passed Congress in 1972 but fell three states short after Schlafly’s campaign against it.

facts.text: Alice Paul wrote the Equal Rights Amendment, first introduced in Congress in 1923.
The ERA passed Congress in 1972 and was ratified by 35 of the 38 states needed.
Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA (“Stop Taking Our Privileges”) argued the amendment would take away protections women already had.
The ERA’s supporters said it would guarantee that equal rights could not be denied “on account of sex.”
The ratification deadline, extended to 1982, passed with the ERA three states short.

title: The 1924 quotas
description: The 1924 act’s national origins quotas favored northern and western Europe and shut out Asia.

facts.text: The Immigration Act of 1924 set each nationality’s quota at 2 percent of its people in the US in the 1890 census.
The 1924 quotas favored immigrants from the British Isles and western Europe and limited those from southern and eastern Europe.
The 1924 act barred immigrants “ineligible for citizenship,” cutting off almost all immigration from Asia.

title: The 1965 Immigration Act
description: The 1965 act replaced quotas with family and skill preferences and changed who came.

facts.text: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended the national origins quotas, favoring people with family in the US and skilled workers.
President Lyndon Johnson signed the act on October 3, 1965, at the foot of the Statue of Liberty.
At the signing, Johnson said the law was “not a revolutionary bill.”
After 1965, immigrants came increasingly from Asia, Africa and Latin America rather than Europe.

title: Watergate: break-in and tapes
description: A 1972 break-in tied to Nixon’s campaign led to hearings that exposed a White House taping system.

facts.text: On June 17, 1972, five burglars were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices in Washington’s Watergate complex.
The burglars were connected to President Richard Nixon’s reelection campaign.
Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein kept investigating the break-in.
On July 16, 1973, at televised Senate hearings, aide Alexander Butterfield revealed a secret White House taping system.

title: Nixon resigns
description: A unanimous Court forced out the tapes, and Nixon resigned in 1974 facing impeachment.

facts.text: On July 24, 1974, in United States v. Nixon, the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 0 that Nixon must hand over the tapes.
Nixon complied, and a tape of June 23, 1972, made public on August 5, caught him trying to halt the FBI’s investigation.
In late July 1974 the House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment against Nixon.
Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, the only US president ever to resign.
On September 8, 1974, President Gerald Ford granted Nixon a full pardon.

title: After Watergate
description: Laws of 1978 required disclosure, created independent counsels and made presidential records public.

facts.text: The Ethics in Government Act of 1978 required officials to disclose their finances and set up independent counsels to investigate top officials.
The Presidential Records Act of 1978 made a president’s official records public property, not private papers.

title: The Cold War and civil rights
description: The Cold War rivalry made segregation a foreign-policy liability, tying the era’s two big stories together.

facts.text: In 1952 the Justice Department told the Court in Brown that “racial discrimination furnishes grist for the Communist propaganda mills.”

title: Fact or interpretation?
description: A fact is a claim you can check against evidence; an interpretation argues why something happened. Historiography studies how those interpretations change.

facts.text: Historiography is the history of history writing: how historians in different times and places have interpreted events differently.

title: Why the colonists rebelled: rival explanations
description: Carl Becker (1909) and the Progressives saw a struggle over home rule and who should rule at home; Bernard Bailyn (1967) traced the Revolution to ideas and a fear of conspiracy against liberty.

facts.text: In 1909 historian Carl Becker argued the Revolution was two struggles: one over home rule, and one over who should rule at home.
Progressive historians such as Becker and Charles Beard read the Revolution as a class struggle and treated the revolutionaries’ rhetoric as largely a cover for their interests.

In The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution (1967), Bernard Bailyn argued colonists’ ideas gave them a strong fear of tyranny and of conspiracies against their liberty, explaining their reaction to Britain’s new policies of the 1760s.
Bailyn based his book on a study of the era’s pamphlets and took the revolutionaries’ ideas seriously, assuming people meant what they wrote.

title: Primary and secondary sources
description: Primary sources were made during the time under study; secondary sources analyze them later. Historians question a primary source: who made it, when, for whom and why.

facts.text: Primary sources are original materials created during the time under study by people who lived through it, such as letters, diaries and official documents.
A secondary source, such as a history book or textbook, analyzes and interprets primary sources and is written after the event.
Historians read a primary source critically rather than as literal truth, asking who wrote it, why, and for what audience.

title: Douglass’s Fourth of July speech
description: On July 5, 1852, in Rochester, Frederick Douglass asked what the Fourth of July meant to an enslaved American, while praising the founders and calling the Constitution a liberty document.

facts.text: On July 5, 1852, Frederick Douglass spoke at Corinthian Hall in Rochester, New York, at the invitation of the Rochester Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society.
About 500 to 600 people attended Douglass’s speech and heartily supported his message.
Douglass asked, “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?” and said it reveals “the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.”
Douglass told his audience: “This Fourth [of] July is yours, not mine. You may rejoice, I must mourn.”
Douglass said “the conscience of the nation must be roused.”
In the same speech Douglass called the signers of the Declaration “brave men” and said the Constitution, “interpreted as it ought to be interpreted,” is “a GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT.”

title: The evidence on secession
description: The seceding states’ declarations of causes and Confederate leaders’ speeches in 1860 and 1861 named slavery as the reason for secession.

facts.text: Four seceding states, Texas, Mississippi, Georgia and South Carolina, issued declarations of causes explaining why they left the Union.
South Carolina’s declaration complained that Northern states had passed laws that nullified the federal acts for returning people who escaped slavery, or made them useless.

In his Cornerstone Speech of March 21, 1861, Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens said the new government’s cornerstone rested on slavery and the claim that Black people were not equal to white people.

title: The Lost Cause interpretation
description: After the war, Lost Cause writers claimed secession was about states’ rights, not slavery; historians largely consider these beliefs false.

facts.text: After the war, Lost Cause writers claimed that secession had little or nothing to do with slavery and was about states’ rights.
Lost Cause writers focused on political disputes over states’ rights, ignoring the fact that the rights in question concerned slavery.
Historians largely consider the Lost Cause beliefs false.

title: The Dunning School
description: William A. Dunning of Columbia and his students portrayed Reconstruction as a mistake, blaming Black officeholders, “scalawags” and “carpetbaggers.”

facts.text: William Archibald Dunning, a Columbia University historian, shaped popular understanding of Reconstruction through his writings and the historians he trained.
The Dunning School called Reconstruction a mistake, claiming ill-prepared Black officeholders, Southern white “scalawags” and Northern “carpetbaggers” brought havoc on the South.

title: Du Bois’s Black Reconstruction
description: In 1935 W. E. B. Du Bois showed freedpeople actively shaped Reconstruction; revisionist scholars later overturned the Dunning School.

facts.text: In Black Reconstruction (1935), W. E. B. Du Bois showed that freedpeople actively shaped Reconstruction’s politics and its advances in civil rights and democracy.
Building on the gains of the civil rights movement, revisionist scholars overturned the Dunning School’s picture of Reconstruction.
Eric Foner of Columbia University writes that Reconstruction, long portrayed as a sordid time, has lately been viewed as a laudable experiment in interracial democracy.
Southern Reconstruction governments offered lavish aid to railroads, and the program spawned corruption and rising taxes that alienated many white voters.

title: The New Deal’s record
description: Roosevelt took office with about a quarter of workers jobless; output recovered by 1937, but unemployment stayed above 10 percent until the war brought full employment.

facts.text: When Franklin D. Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, the banking system had collapsed and nearly 25 percent of the labor force was unemployed.
Among the New Deal’s programs was Social Security, created in 1935.
By 1937 the recovery had pushed output, income and manufacturing back to 1929 levels, writes Richard A. Walker of the Living New Deal.
Unemployment stayed above 10 percent through the New Deal years, and World War II brought full employment.

title: New Deal critics, right and left
description: The American Liberty League (1934) said Roosevelt did too much; Huey Long’s Share Our Wealth said the New Deal did too little.

facts.text: In August 1934 conservatives organized the American Liberty League, arguing Roosevelt had done too much and accusing him of creeping socialism.
Senator Huey Long of Louisiana said the New Deal did not do enough, and in 1934 founded the Share Our Wealth Society to limit big fortunes and guarantee families a minimum.

title: The atomic bombings of 1945
description: The US bombed Hiroshima on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9, 1945; Japan surrendered within days.

facts.text: On August 6, 1945, the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and on August 9 a second on Nagasaki.
Estimates of deaths in Hiroshima by the end of 1945 range from 90,000 to 166,000.
Japan surrendered within days of the Nagasaki bombing, in mid-August 1945.

title: Why the bombs were used: the debate
description: Traditionalists (after Stimson, 1947) say the bombs saved lives by avoiding an invasion; revisionists (after Alperovitz, 1965) say they were unnecessary and aimed at the Soviets; many historians stand between.

facts.text: In a 1947 Harper’s Magazine article, former Secretary of War Henry Stimson defended the decision, pointing to Japan’s refusal to surrender and the cost of an invasion.
Historians called traditionalists argue the bombs were necessary to save American lives and prevent an invasion of Japan.

In 1965 historian Gar Alperovitz argued the bombs were not needed to force Japan’s surrender, since Japan was already close to it, and were meant mainly to strengthen the US hand against the Soviet Union.
Some US policymakers hoped the bomb’s demonstrated power might push the Soviets to make concessions.
Criticizing both camps, historian J. Samuel Walker concluded that the main motive for using the bombs was to end the war as quickly as possible.
Many historians take positions between the traditionalists and the revisionists.

title: How the Cold War ended
description: Gorbachev (from 1985) needed to cut military spending; he and Reagan signed the INF Treaty in 1987; the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the Soviet Union ended in December 1991.

facts.text: Mikhail Gorbachev became the Soviet leader in March 1985 and inherited a stagnant economy.
To restructure the Soviet economy, Gorbachev needed to reduce military spending at home and political tensions abroad.
Reagan and Gorbachev held four summit meetings between 1985 and 1988, and in December 1987 signed the INF Treaty, which eliminated an entire class of missiles.
The first revolution of 1989 came in Poland, where the Solidarity movement won freer elections.
Gorbachev’s decision to loosen Soviet control of Eastern Europe fed the movement that brought down the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and Communist rule across Eastern Europe.
On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin for the last time.

title: Why the Cold War ended: explanations
description: Historians weigh Reagan’s buildup and SDI, unrest in Eastern Europe, the Afghan war and the Soviet economy, and have reached no consensus.

facts.text: Some historians credit Reagan’s military buildup and his Strategic Defense Initiative; others stress unrest in Eastern Europe, especially Poland, and Soviet overreach in Afghanistan; others the Soviet economy’s implosion.
Historians have reached no consensus on how much weight each of these factors deserves.
The State Department’s historians write that Gorbachev took the initiative in arms control, and Reagan was well prepared to negotiate.

title: The attacks of September 11, 2001
description: Nineteen al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four planes; they struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, Flight 93 crashed in Pennsylvania, and 2,977 people were killed.

facts.text: On the morning of September 11, 2001, 19 terrorists from al-Qaeda, an Islamist extremist group, hijacked four commercial airplanes.
The hijackers crashed two planes into the North and South Towers of the World Trade Center in New York and a third into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.
On the fourth plane, Flight 93, passengers fought back after learning of the other attacks, and the plane crashed into a field in western Pennsylvania.
The attacks killed 2,977 people: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93.

title: Why recent history is harder
description: Many records of recent events stay closed for years; under the Presidential Records Act public requests open five years after an administration, with some restrictions up to 12 years.

facts.text: Under the Presidential Records Act, the public can request a president’s records five years after the administration ends, but some may be restricted for up to 12 years.

title: How American myths are made
description: Weems invented the cherry tree (1806), Longfellow’s 1860 poem reshaped Revere’s ride, and Canby’s 1870 paper launched the Betsy Ross flag story.

facts.text: The cherry tree story was invented by Mason Locke “Parson” Weems, whose Washington biography first appeared in 1800, a year after Washington’s death; the story was added in the fifth edition of 1806.
Weems’s biography became a bestseller read by generations of American schoolchildren.
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem “Paul Revere’s Ride” was published in December 1860, taking significant poetic license with the facts.
Longfellow wrote the poem in a time of growing national crisis between North and South.
William Dawes and Samuel Prescott also rode that night; a British patrol stopped all three, Dawes and Prescott escaped, and Revere was held.
Revere did not ride alone: he was one of two riders to leave Boston, and he was captured by British regulars in Lincoln and never reached Concord.
The story that Betsy Ross made the first flag was made public by her grandson William Canby in 1870, in a paper to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania drawing on family stories.
There is no firm evidence that Betsy Ross designed or made the first flag, though she did make flags for the navy.
